system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: The NFRs (read-heavy, low-latency redirects, durable writes) are what push you toward a cache in front of a key-value store — not the feature list.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Scalability is a system's ability to keep working well as the amount of work grows.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Scalability?

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: But there is a hard ceiling (the biggest machine you can buy) and it is a single point of failure.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Scalability?

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Keeping a user's session or uploaded file on one machine breaks the moment the load balancer sends their next request elsewhere.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Scalability?

“"Work" usually means more users, more requests per second, more data, or bigger ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: "Work" usually means more users, more requests per second, more data, or bigger responses.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Availability is the share of time a system is up and able to serve requests.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Availability?

“The biggest enemy is the ____: any one component that, when it dies, takes the whole system with it.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: The biggest enemy is the single point of failure (SPOF): any one component that, when it dies, takes the whole system with it.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Availability?

“If your ____ is meant to run 24/7 and it was unreachable for 43 minutes last month, that month's availability was about 99.9%.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: If your service is meant to run 24/7 and it was unreachable for 43 minutes last month, that month's availability was about 99.9%.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Availability?

“Five app servers behind a ____ still go dark if they all point at a single database.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Five app servers behind a load balancer still go dark if they all point at a single database.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Availability?

“____ on the weakest link buys the most availability.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Redundancy on the weakest link buys the most availability.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Reliability?

“____ is the system doing the right thing — correct results, no lost data — continuously over time, even when parts fail.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Reliability is the system doing the right thing — correct results, no lost data — continuously over time, even when parts fail.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Reliability?

“Failures come from three places: ____ (disks, memory, power), software (bugs, bad deploys, memory leaks), and humans (wrong config, fat-fingered command).”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Failures come from three places: hardware (disks, memory, power), software (bugs, bad deploys, memory leaks), and humans (wrong config, fat-fingered command).

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Reliability?

“If a ____ fails on average every 30 days and takes 1 hour to fully recover:”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: If a service fails on average every 30 days and takes 1 hour to fully recover:

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Reliability?

“Attach an ____ key so the server ignores the duplicate.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Attach an idempotency key so the server ignores the duplicate.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Reliability?

“You do not always need fewer ____ — recovering faster (lower MTTR) is often the cheaper path to more nines.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: You do not always need fewer failures — recovering faster (lower MTTR) is often the cheaper path to more nines.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?

“A ____ (SPOF) is any one component whose failure takes down the entire system.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any one component whose failure takes down the entire system.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?

“Find them, then remove them — that is most of ____ engineering.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Find them, then remove them — that is most of availability engineering.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?

“____ end to end, including DNS, CDN, load balancer, app, cache, database, and any third-party call.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Draw the request path end to end, including DNS, CDN, load balancer, app, cache, database, and any third-party call.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?

“Many app servers, one database or one ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Many app servers, one database or one load balancer.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?

“____ only counts if the two copies fail independently.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Redundancy only counts if the two copies fail independently.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Latency Throughput and Bandwidth?

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Three different measurements of a system's speed: latency is how long one request takes, throughput is how many requests finish per second, and bandwidth is the maximum data rate the pipe can carry.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Latency Throughput and Bandwidth?

“Track p50 (median), p95, and p99 — the time that 50%, 95%, 99% of ____ beat.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Track p50 (median), p95, and p99 — the time that 50%, 95%, 99% of requests beat.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Latency Throughput and Bandwidth?

“Target throughput: 1,000 requests/second at ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Target throughput: 1,000 requests/second at peak.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Latency Throughput and Bandwidth?

“A healthy mean with an ugly ____ means a slice of users are having a bad time.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: A healthy mean with an ugly p99 means a slice of users are having a bad time.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Latency Throughput and Bandwidth?

“____ = throughput × latency (L = λ × W)”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: concurrency = throughput × latency (L = λ × W)

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“____ is a way to spread keys (cache entries, user data, files) across a set of servers so that adding or removing a server moves as few keys as possible.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Consistent hashing is a way to spread keys (cache entries, user data, files) across a set of servers so that adding or removing a server moves as few keys as possible.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“Going from 4 to 5 ____ moves about 80% of them.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Going from 4 to 5 servers moves about 80% of them.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“____ from 55: the next server point is S3 at 90. user:42 lives on S3.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Walk clockwise from 55: the next server point is S3 at 90. user:42 lives on S3.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“Real systems also copy each key to the next 2–3 servers clockwise for ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Real systems also copy each key to the next 2–3 servers clockwise for redundancy.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“Modulo ____ moves ~1 - 1/N of keys on every change.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Modulo hashing moves ~1 - 1/N of keys on every change.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“The CAP theorem says that when a distributed system hits a network partition, it must choose between consistency and ____ — it cannot keep both.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: The CAP theorem says that when a distributed system hits a network partition, it must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot keep both.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“PACELC adds: else (no partition), a system still trades latency vs ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: PACELC adds: else (no partition), a system still trades latency vs consistency.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“Showing stale money or allowing a double-spend is unacceptable → CP: refuse the operation during a ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Showing stale money or allowing a double-spend is unacceptable → CP: refuse the operation during a partition.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“A single-node database is CA, but the moment you replicate across machines, ____ are possible and CA is off the table.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: A single-node database is CA, but the moment you replicate across machines, partitions are possible and CA is off the table.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“The three letters: C onsistency (every read sees the latest write), A vailability (every request gets a non-error response), P artition tolerance (the system keeps working when the ____ between nodes breaks).”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: The three letters: C onsistency (every read sees the latest write), A vailability (every request gets a non-error response), P artition tolerance (the system keeps working when the network between nodes breaks).

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistency Models?

“Once data is copied to more than one machine, a ____ model is the rule for when readers are guaranteed to see the latest write.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Once data is copied to more than one machine, a consistency model is the rule for when readers are guaranteed to see the latest write.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistency Models?

“When replicas cannot talk to each other (a network partition), a system must choose: reject requests to stay ____, or keep serving with possibly-stale data to stay available.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: When replicas cannot talk to each other (a network partition), a system must choose: reject requests to stay consistent, or keep serving with possibly-stale data to stay available.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistency Models?

“Selling the same seat twice is a real problem → ____ for the final booking step.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Selling the same seat twice is a real problem → strong for the final booking step.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistency Models?

“If your app reads from a replica right after writing to the ____, it can read its own stale data.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: If your app reads from a replica right after writing to the primary, it can read its own stale data.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistency Models?

“Most real systems are a mix: strong consistency on the few operations that touch money or inventory, ____ everywhere else.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Most real systems are a mix: strong consistency on the few operations that touch money or inventory, eventual everywhere else.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Capacity Estimation?

“Capacity ____ is working out — before you build — roughly how many requests per second, how much storage, and how much bandwidth a system will need.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Capacity estimation is working out — before you build — roughly how many requests per second, how much storage, and how much bandwidth a system will need.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Capacity Estimation?

“Most consumer apps are ____ (often 100:1 or more).”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Most consumer apps are read-heavy (often 100:1 or more).

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Capacity Estimation?

“In an ____ you are asked to design a Twitter-like feed.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: In an interview you are asked to design a Twitter-like feed.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Capacity Estimation?

“Sizing for the daily ____ means you are under-provisioned every lunchtime and every evening.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Sizing for the daily average means you are under-provisioned every lunchtime and every evening.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Capacity Estimation?

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Two conclusions fell out for free: reads are ~50× writes so a cache + CDN is mandatory, and 33 PB means object storage (like S3), never a single database.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations?

“A back-of-the-envelope calculation is fast, rough arithmetic to check whether a ____ idea is even plausible — done in your head or on a napkin, in under a minute.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: A back-of-the-envelope calculation is fast, rough arithmetic to check whether a design idea is even plausible — done in your head or on a napkin, in under a minute.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations?

“1 char ≈ 1 byte; a typical short ____ record ≈ a few hundred bytes.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: 1 char ≈ 1 byte; a typical short JSON record ≈ a few hundred bytes.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations?

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations?

“____ speeds are quoted in bits (Mbps), storage in bytes.”
system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: Network speeds are quoted in bits (Mbps), storage in bytes.

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations?

system-design-fundamentals/core-concepts.explanation: The pattern: pick round inputs → multiply/divide with powers of ten → compare the result to a known limit (RAM size, one server's QPS, a disk).

Which term completes this statement from IP Addresses and Subnets?

system-design-fundamentals/networking--i.explanation: 192.168.1.0/24 means "the first 24 bits are the network, the last 8 identify the host". 8 host bits → 2 8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are usable (one is the network address, one is broadcast).

system-design-fundamentals/networking--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from IP Addresses and Subnets?

“/22 = 22 ____ bits → the mask is 255.255.252.0.”

Which term completes this statement from IP Addresses and Subnets?

“If it has a route to an internet ____, it is reachable from the internet.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--i.explanation: If it has a route to an internet gateway, it is reachable from the internet.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from IP Addresses and Subnets?

“No match → hand the packet to the default gateway (____).”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--i.explanation: No match → hand the packet to the default gateway (router).

system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.prompt: What does DNS primarily do when you open a website?
options: Translate a domain name into an address
Balance CPU usage inside a server
system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.explanation: DNS resolves human-readable names to records such as IP addresses that clients can use to connect.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.prompt: Which DNS record aliases one name to another name?
system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.explanation: A CNAME points to another domain name. A and AAAA hold IP addresses; MX identifies mail servers.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.prompt: Which server holds the domain owner’s DNS records?
system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.explanation: Authoritative nameservers publish the records for their zones. A recursive resolver discovers and caches answers.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.prompt: You plan a DNS cutover tomorrow. What helps reduce how long clients retain the old address?
options: Raise the TTL during the cutover
Delete every cache on the internet
Lower the TTL early enough for the old TTL to expire
system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.explanation: Resolvers that cached the old TTL may keep it until it expires. Lower the TTL in advance so later responses expire sooner.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.prompt: What is the main trade-off of a low DNS TTL?
options: Faster refreshes, but more DNS lookups
It removes the need for authoritative servers
system-design-fundamentals/networking--d.explanation: A short TTL reduces cache lifetime but increases query traffic. Updates still depend on caches and client behavior.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from TCP and UDP?

“TCP and UDP are the two ways to actually send ____ over IP.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.explanation: TCP and UDP are the two ways to actually send data over IP.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from TCP and UDP?

“Ordering: each byte has a ____ number; the receiver reassembles in order.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.explanation: Ordering: each byte has a sequence number; the receiver reassembles in order.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from TCP and UDP?

“____ and UDP sit on top and decide how much effort to spend making delivery dependable.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.explanation: TCP and UDP sit on top and decide how much effort to spend making delivery dependable.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from TCP and UDP?

“Paying the handshake (and ____) every time adds one or more round trips.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.explanation: Paying the handshake (and TLS) every time adds one or more round trips.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from TCP and UDP?

“Reach for UDP only when the ____ cost of waiting for a lost packet is worse than the data loss itself — then be ready to handle loss in your app.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--t.explanation: Reach for UDP only when the latency cost of waiting for a lost packet is worse than the data loss itself — then be ready to handle loss in your app.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from HTTP and HTTPS?

“HTTP is the request/response language of the web: a client asks for a resource, a ____ answers.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.explanation: HTTP is the request/response language of the web: a client asks for a resource, a server answers.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from HTTP and HTTPS?

“The response mirrors it: a status line ( HTTP/1.1 201 Created ), ____, blank line, body.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.explanation: The response mirrors it: a status line ( HTTP/1.1 201 Created ), headers, blank line, body.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from HTTP and HTTPS?

“Server replies ____ with ETag: "abc123" and Cache-Control: max-age=3600.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.explanation: Server replies 200 OK with ETag: "abc123" and Cache-Control: max-age=3600.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from HTTP and HTTPS?

“200 OK with {"error":"not found"} breaks caching, ____, and clients.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.explanation: 200 OK with {"error":"not found"} breaks caching, monitoring, and clients.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from HTTP and HTTPS?

“HTTP is ____ — each request stands alone. "Sessions" are rebuilt every request from a cookie or token the client re-sends.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--h.explanation: HTTP is stateless — each request stands alone. "Sessions" are rebuilt every request from a cookie or token the client re-sends.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from WebSockets?

“A WebSocket is a single long-lived, two-way ____ between browser and server.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.explanation: A WebSocket is a single long-lived, two-way connection between browser and server.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from WebSockets?

“If the server agrees, it replies ____ and the same TCP connection stops speaking HTTP and starts speaking the WebSocket frame protocol.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.explanation: If the server agrees, it replies 101 Switching Protocols and the same TCP connection stops speaking HTTP and starts speaking the WebSocket frame protocol.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from WebSockets?

“Connect: browser opens new ____("wss://app.example.com/doc/42").”

Which term completes this statement from WebSockets?

“Proxies and phones silently drop idle ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.explanation: Proxies and phones silently drop idle connections.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from WebSockets?

“The server now holds state (which socket is in which room), so scaling ____ means a shared pub/sub layer (like Redis) so any server can reach any client.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--w.explanation: The server now holds state (which socket is in which room), so scaling WebSockets means a shared pub/sub layer (like Redis) so any server can reach any client.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a globe-spanning network of caching servers that keep copies of your content close to users, so ____ are served from a nearby city instead of your origin server.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a globe-spanning network of caching servers that keep copies of your content close to users, so requests are served from a nearby city instead of your origin server.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“The fix is a ____: style.9f2a1c.css.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: The fix is a content hash in the filename: style.9f2a1c.css.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“DNS points to the CDN. cdn.____.com resolves to the CDN, which returns the IP of the nearest edge (anycast / geo-DNS).”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: DNS points to the CDN. cdn.example.com resolves to the CDN, which returns the IP of the nearest edge (anycast / geo-DNS).

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“Without ____, many CDNs will not cache at all, or cache unpredictably.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: Without Cache-Control, many CDNs will not cache at all, or cache unpredictably.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“A good cache-hit ratio (often 90%+ for static sites) means your origin can be small and cheap — the CDN absorbs the ____ and the spikes.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: A good cache-hit ratio (often 90%+ for static sites) means your origin can be small and cheap — the CDN absorbs the traffic and the spikes.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OSI Model?

“Real systems use the simpler 4-layer TCP/IP model, but OSI's vocabulary ("that is a layer 7 ____", "a layer 2 switch") is everywhere.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.explanation: Real systems use the simpler 4-layer TCP/IP model, but OSI's vocabulary ("that is a layer 7 load balancer", "a layer 2 switch") is everywhere.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OSI Model?

“The TCP/IP model collapses OSI into four: ____ (OSI 5–7), Transport (4), Internet (3), Link (1–2).”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.explanation: The TCP/IP model collapses OSI into four: Application (OSI 5–7), Transport (4), Internet (3), Link (1–2).

system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OSI Model?

“L4: TCP wraps it in a segment, adds source/destination ports, ____ numbers.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.explanation: L4: TCP wraps it in a segment, adds source/destination ports, sequence numbers.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OSI Model?

“Real stacks do not have clean layer 5 and 6 ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.explanation: Real stacks do not have clean layer 5 and 6 components.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OSI Model?

“That is why you can swap wifi for ethernet (L1/L2) without changing a line of your ____ code (L7).”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--o.explanation: That is why you can swap wifi for ethernet (L1/L2) without changing a line of your HTTP code (L7).

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Checksums?

“A checksum is a small value computed from a block of ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: A checksum is a small value computed from a block of data.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Checksums?

“A corrupted ____ segment fails its checksum and is silently retransmitted — you never see it.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: A corrupted TCP segment fails its checksum and is silently retransmitted — you never see it.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Checksums?

“____ computes sha256(app-1.2.0.zip) and publishes it next to the file.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: Publisher computes sha256(app-1.2.0.zip) and publishes it next to the file.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Checksums?

“If tampering is a concern, use SHA-256 and ideally a ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: If tampering is a concern, use SHA-256 and ideally a signature.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Checksums?

“TCP's checksum protects the wire; an application hash protects everything else — disk writes, proxies, CDN caches, and ____ that TCP never saw.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--c.explanation: TCP's checksum protects the wire; an application hash protects everything else — disk writes, proxies, CDN caches, and storage that TCP never saw.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Proxy vs Reverse Proxy?

“The difference is whose side they are on: a ____ acts for the client; a reverse proxy acts for the server.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.explanation: The difference is whose side they are on: a forward proxy acts for the client; a reverse proxy acts for the server.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Proxy vs Reverse Proxy?

“Load balancer: a ____ whose main job is spreading traffic.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.explanation: Load balancer: a reverse proxy whose main job is spreading traffic.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Proxy vs Reverse Proxy?

“DNS for shop.____.com points at the reverse proxy's IP, not any backend.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.explanation: DNS for shop.example.com points at the reverse proxy's IP, not any backend.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Proxy vs Reverse Proxy?

“Without ____ (and the backend trusting it), every request looks like it came from the proxy — breaking rate limits and analytics.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.explanation: Without X-Forwarded-For (and the backend trusting it), every request looks like it came from the proxy — breaking rate limits and analytics.

system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Proxy vs Reverse Proxy?

“The reverse proxy is where you put every cross-cutting concern — TLS, caching, ____, auth, rate limiting, routing — so backend code stays simple and hidden.”
system-design-fundamentals/networking--p.explanation: The reverse proxy is where you put every cross-cutting concern — TLS, caching, compression, auth, rate limiting, routing — so backend code stays simple and hidden.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What are Load Balancers??

“It gives you one stable address to point users at, while the pool of ____ behind it can grow, shrink, or fail without users noticing.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: It gives you one stable address to point users at, while the pool of servers behind it can grow, shrink, or fail without users noticing.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What are Load Balancers??

“Hardware / dedicated appliances — older ____ centres (F5, Citrix).”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Hardware / dedicated appliances — older data centres (F5, Citrix).

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What are Load Balancers??

“DNS resolves app.example.com to the ____'s IP.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: DNS resolves app.example.com to the load balancer's IP.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What are Load Balancers??

“If user data lives on one ____, the LB sending the next request elsewhere logs the user out.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: If user data lives on one server, the LB sending the next request elsewhere logs the user out.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What are Load Balancers??

“A single load balancer is itself a ____ — production setups run at least two, with a floating IP or DNS failover between them.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure — production setups run at least two, with a floating IP or DNS failover between them.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing Algorithms?

“A ____ algorithm is the rule the load balancer uses to pick which server gets the next request.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A load balancing algorithm is the rule the load balancer uses to pick which server gets the next request.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing Algorithms?

“Prefer a shared session store and keep the LB ____ where you can.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Prefer a shared session store and keep the LB stateless where you can.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing Algorithms?

“The right choice depends on whether your ____ are all similar or wildly uneven.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: The right choice depends on whether your requests are all similar or wildly uneven.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing Algorithms?

“A few slow endpoints turn a "fair" rotation into an unfair one — new work lands on ____ already stuck.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A few slow endpoints turn a "fair" rotation into an unfair one — new work lands on servers already stuck.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing Algorithms?

“Default to ____ for HTTP services — it self-corrects when a server slows down, which round robin cannot.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Default to least connections for HTTP services — it self-corrects when a server slows down, which round robin cannot.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing?

“A Layer 4 ____ routes using only the IP address and port.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A Layer 4 load balancer routes using only the IP address and port.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing?

“A ____ load balancer opens the request and routes using the URL, headers, and cookies.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A Layer 7 load balancer opens the request and routes using the URL, headers, and cookies.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing?

“____ (a database proxy, a game server, gRPC streams where you do not need routing) → Layer 4.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Just spreading raw TCP traffic (a database proxy, a game server, gRPC streams where you do not need routing) → Layer 4.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing?

“Parsing and TLS on a firehose of traffic that needs no routing just adds ____ and cost.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Parsing and TLS on a firehose of traffic that needs no routing just adds latency and cost.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing?

“If you never need to look inside the request, ____ is faster and simpler.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: If you never need to look inside the request, Layer 4 is faster and simpler.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from DNS Load Balancing?

“DNS ____ spreads traffic by giving different users different answers to the same name lookup.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: DNS load balancing spreads traffic by giving different users different answers to the same name lookup.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from DNS Load Balancing?

“The DNS ____ decides which one(s) to return and in what order, using one of these strategies:”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: The DNS server decides which one(s) to return and in what order, using one of these strategies:

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from DNS Load Balancing?

“Setup: example.com has two A records — 1.1.1.1 (US, primary) and 2.2.2.2 (EU, standby) — with a health-checked ____ policy and a 60s TTL.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Setup: example.com has two A records — 1.1.1.1 (US, primary) and 2.2.2.2 (EU, standby) — with a health-checked failover policy and a 60s TTL.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from DNS Load Balancing?

“A 1-hour TTL means a dead region keeps taking ____ for up to an hour.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A 1-hour TTL means a dead region keeps taking traffic for up to an hour.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from DNS Load Balancing?

“Use a real ____ inside each region for per-request distribution.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Use a real load balancer inside each region for per-request distribution.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Anycast Routing?

“Anycast routing lets many servers in different cities share the ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Anycast routing lets many servers in different cities share the same IP address.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Anycast Routing?

“____ with zero client logic and no DNS TTL to wait on.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Automatic nearest routing with zero client logic and no DNS TTL to wait on.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Anycast Routing?

“____ announces the prefix containing 1.1.1.1 to its local internet providers via BGP.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Every resolver site announces the prefix containing 1.1.1.1 to its local internet providers via BGP.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Anycast Routing?

“A route flap moves your packets to a location with no session state and the TCP ____ resets.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: A route flap moves your packets to a location with no session state and the TCP connection resets.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Anycast Routing?

“Anycast = "let the internet do the ____." Great for global reach and resilience on short requests; combine it with regional load balancers for the actual app servers.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Anycast = "let the internet do the load balancing." Great for global reach and resilience on short requests; combine it with regional load balancers for the actual app servers.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Health Checks and Failover?

“____ are the detection; failover is the reaction.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Health checks are the detection; failover is the reaction.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Health Checks and Failover?

“____ — how often to check (e.g. every 5s).”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Interval — how often to check (e.g. every 5s).

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Health Checks and Failover?

“Steady state: 3 ____, each passing /health every 5s.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Steady state: 3 servers, each passing /health every 5s.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Health Checks and Failover?

“Check the ____ that requests actually need.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Check the dependencies that requests actually need.

system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Health Checks and Failover?

“____ is only safe if the remaining servers have the spare capacity to carry the load.”
system-design-fundamentals/load-balancin.explanation: Failover is only safe if the remaining servers have the spare capacity to carry the load.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is an API??

“An API (Application Programming ____) is a contract that lets one piece of software ask another to do something or return data — without knowing how it works inside.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.explanation: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract that lets one piece of software ask another to do something or return data — without knowing how it works inside.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is an API??

“In system ____, "API" almost always means a web API over HTTP.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.explanation: In system design, "API" almost always means a web API over HTTP.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is an API??

“Define the response. ____, body = {"id": 501, "status": "pending", "total": 780}, header Location: /orders/501.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.explanation: Define the response. 201 Created, body = {"id": 501, "status": "pending", "total": 780}, header Location: /orders/501.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is an API??

“Map to a response model so storage can change without breaking ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.explanation: Map to a response model so storage can change without breaking clients.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is an API??

“Once other teams build against it, changing its shape breaks them — which is why ____ and careful design matter from day one.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--w.explanation: Once other teams build against it, changing its shape breaks them — which is why versioning and careful design matter from day one.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Idempotency?

“An operation is ____ if doing it once and doing it many times have the exact same effect.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.explanation: An operation is idempotent if doing it once and doing it many times have the exact same effect.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Idempotency?

“The client generates a unique ID (a UUID) for the operation and sends it as a header: ____-Key: 7c3e-...-9f.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.explanation: The client generates a unique ID (a UUID) for the operation and sends it as a header: Idempotency-Key: 7c3e-...-9f.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Idempotency?

“Client creates key = uuid() once, before the first attempt, and keeps it for all ____ of this order.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.explanation: Client creates key = uuid() once, before the first attempt, and keeps it for all retries of this order.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Idempotency?

“If the ____ makes a new UUID for the retry, the server sees a brand-new operation and does it again.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.explanation: If the client makes a new UUID for the retry, the server sees a brand-new operation and does it again.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Idempotency?

“It is the difference between "safe to retry" and "pray the ____ holds".”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--i.explanation: It is the difference between "safe to retry" and "pray the network holds".

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Formats?

“JSON, XML, ____, and others each trade readability for speed and size.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.explanation: JSON, XML, Protocol Buffers, and others each trade readability for speed and size.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Formats?

“____-less (JSON, XML): the data describes itself with field names.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.explanation: Schema-less (JSON, XML): the data describes itself with field names.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Formats?

“Send ____, honour Accept, and document exactly which formats the endpoint supports.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.explanation: Send Content-Type, honour Accept, and document exactly which formats the endpoint supports.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Formats?

“Forcing external developers to compile .proto files for a simple ____ call kills adoption.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.explanation: Forcing external developers to compile .proto files for a simple REST call kills adoption.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Formats?

“Move to a binary, schema-first format when profiling shows serialization or bandwidth is a real ____ — usually only on internal high-volume links.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--d.explanation: Move to a binary, schema-first format when profiling shows serialization or bandwidth is a real bottleneck — usually only on internal high-volume links.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Architectural Styles?

“The big four today are REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and older SOAP — plus event styles like ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.explanation: The big four today are REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and older SOAP — plus event styles like webhooks.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Architectural Styles?

“An API architectural style is the overall shape of how clients and ____ talk.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.explanation: An API architectural style is the overall shape of how clients and servers talk.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Architectural Styles?

“Each optimises for something different: simplicity, flexible queries, raw speed, or strict ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.explanation: Each optimises for something different: simplicity, flexible queries, raw speed, or strict contracts.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Architectural Styles?

“You take on ____ complexity, query-cost analysis, and hard caching to solve a problem you did not have.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.explanation: You take on resolver complexity, query-cost analysis, and hard caching to solve a problem you did not have.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Architectural Styles?

“Reach for ____ to solve a real client data-fetching pain, and gRPC to solve a real internal performance pain.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--a.explanation: Reach for GraphQL to solve a real client data-fetching pain, and gRPC to solve a real internal performance pain.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from REST API Design?

“REST is a style for HTTP APIs built around resources (nouns) that you act on with standard ____ (verbs).”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.explanation: REST is a style for HTTP APIs built around resources (nouns) that you act on with standard HTTP methods (verbs).

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from REST API Design?

“Use status codes honestly: 201 on create, 404 when missing, 409 on conflict, 422 on ____ errors.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.explanation: Use status codes honestly: 201 on create, 404 when missing, 409 on conflict, 422 on validation errors.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from REST API Design?

“Create: POST /posts/12/comments body {"body": "Nice!"} → 201, ____: /comments/501.”

Which term completes this statement from REST API Design?

“Prefer a state ____: PATCH /orders/42 with {"status": "cancelled"}.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.explanation: Prefer a state change: PATCH /orders/42 with {"status": "cancelled"}.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from REST API Design?

“A REST API is well designed when a developer can predict an ____ they have never seen from the pattern of the ones they have.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--r.explanation: A REST API is well designed when a developer can predict an endpoint they have never seen from the pattern of the ones they have.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from GraphQL Deep Dive?

“The ____ one request describing exactly which fields it wants, and the server returns that shape — nothing more, nothing less.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: The client sends one request describing exactly which fields it wants, and the server returns that shape — nothing more, nothing less.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from GraphQL Deep Dive?

“There is one ____ ( /graphql ), one HTTP method (usually POST), and a schema that defines every type and field the API offers.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: There is one endpoint ( /graphql ), one HTTP method (usually POST), and a schema that defines every type and field the API offers.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from GraphQL Deep Dive?

“Client sends the query string to POST /____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: Client sends the query string to POST /graphql.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from GraphQL Deep Dive?

“Batch with ____ or equivalent from day one.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: Batch with DataLoader or equivalent from day one.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from GraphQL Deep Dive?

“A profile screen needs the ____'s name, their last 3 orders, and each order's total.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: A profile screen needs the user's name, their last 3 orders, and each order's total.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from gRPC Deep Dive?

“gRPC is a way for ____ to call each other like local functions.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: gRPC is a way for services to call each other like local functions.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from gRPC Deep Dive?

“Run the compiler and you get a typed ____ and a server stub.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: Run the compiler and you get a typed CatalogClient and a server stub.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from gRPC Deep Dive?

“Edit the .proto: add rpc GetItems(ItemRequest) returns (ItemList); and the ____, each field with a fresh number.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: Edit the .proto: add rpc GetItems(ItemRequest) returns (ItemList); and the messages, each field with a fresh number.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from gRPC Deep Dive?

“You need grpc-web plus a ____ — often not worth it versus a thin REST layer.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: You need grpc-web plus a proxy — often not worth it versus a thin REST layer.

system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from gRPC Deep Dive?

“gRPC shines inside your system: same company, low latency, many languages, strict ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-design--g.explanation: gRPC shines inside your system: same company, low latency, many languages, strict contracts.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Gateways?

“An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of many backend ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of many backend services.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Gateways?

“____: spreads traffic across identical copies of one service.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Load balancer: spreads traffic across identical copies of one service.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Gateways?

“Client sends GET /v1/orders/42 with ____: Bearer … to api.example.com.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Client sends GET /v1/orders/42 with Authorization: Bearer … to api.example.com.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Gateways?

“Pricing rules or workflow logic creeping into the gateway makes it a ____ and a deploy chokepoint.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Pricing rules or workflow logic creeping into the gateway makes it a bottleneck and a deploy chokepoint.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from API Gateways?

“A gateway removes duplicated plumbing from every ____ — but it is also a critical shared component, so run it redundantly and keep its logic thin.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: A gateway removes duplicated plumbing from every service — but it is also a critical shared component, so run it redundantly and keep its logic thin.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Over the limit, the API replies ____ instead of doing the work.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Over the limit, the API replies 429 Too Many Requests instead of doing the work.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Key by: ____ key or user ID (best), IP (rough — NAT groups users), or a mix.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Key by: API key or user ID (best), IP (rough — NAT groups users), or a mix.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Store per-key state in Redis: tokens and ____ time.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Store per-key state in Redis: tokens and last_refill time.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“With 5 ____ nodes and a "100/min" limit each, the real limit is 500/min and uneven.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: With 5 gateway nodes and a "100/min" limit each, the real limit is 500/min and uneven.

system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Rate limiting usually lives at the API gateway so it is enforced once, before any backend work, and consistently across every ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-infrastru.explanation: Rate limiting usually lives at the API gateway so it is enforced once, before any backend work, and consistently across every service.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication vs Authorization?

“You can be authenticated (we know it is you) and still not authorized (you cannot delete that ____).”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: You can be authenticated (we know it is you) and still not authorized (you cannot delete that document).

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication vs Authorization?

“RBAC (role-based): users have roles ( admin, editor ); roles have ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: RBAC (role-based): users have roles ( admin, editor ); roles have permissions.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication vs Authorization?

“Client sends DELETE /projects/12 with ____: Bearer ….”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Client sends DELETE /projects/12 with Authorization: Bearer ….

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication vs Authorization?

“"They have a valid ____" is not "they may do this".”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: "They have a valid token" is not "they may do this".

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication vs Authorization?

“Returning the wrong one confuses ____ and leaks information.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Returning the wrong one confuses clients and leaks information.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Session vs Token Based Auth?

“Two approaches: ____ (the server keeps the state) and token-based (the client carries the state).”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Two approaches: session-based (the server keeps the state) and token-based (the client carries the state).

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Session vs Token Based Auth?

“After you log in, the ____ needs to remember it is you on every later request.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: After you log in, the server needs to remember it is you on every later request.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Session vs Token Based Auth?

“Session — login: verify credentials, create a session row {sid: abc, userId: 7, expires}, send Set-Cookie: sid=abc; ____; Secure; SameSite.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Session — login: verify credentials, create a session row {sid: abc, userId: 7, expires}, send Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Session vs Token Based Auth?

“Keep access ____ to minutes and use refresh ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Keep access tokens to minutes and use refresh tokens.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Session vs Token Based Auth?

“Short access token + ____ is the common middle ground: you get token scalability and keep the blast radius of a leaked token small.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Short access token + refresh token is the common middle ground: you get token scalability and keep the blast radius of a leaked token small.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from JWT?

“A JWT (JSON Web ____) is a compact, signed piece of JSON that proves a set of claims — typically "this is user 7, and this ____ is valid until 3:45 PM".”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, signed piece of JSON that proves a set of claims — typically "this is user 7, and this token is valid until 3:45 PM".

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from JWT?

“The ____ is what stops tampering: change one character of the payload and the ____ no longer matches.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: The signature is what stops tampering: change one character of the payload and the signature no longer matches.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from JWT?

“Login: the auth server checks the ____, then builds a payload {sub, role, iss, aud, exp: now+15m}.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Login: the auth server checks the password, then builds a payload {sub, role, iss, aud, exp: now+15m}.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from JWT?

“No ____, no PII beyond an ID, no internal flags you would not show the user.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: No passwords, no PII beyond an ID, no internal flags you would not show the user.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from JWT?

“Keep the lifetime short and always send it over ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Keep the lifetime short and always send it over HTTPS.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OAuth / OAuth2?

“OAuth 2.0 is a protocol for ____: it lets you give App A permission to use some of your data on Service B — without giving App A your Service B password.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is a protocol for delegated access: it lets you give App A permission to use some of your data on Service B — without giving App A your Service B password.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OAuth / OAuth2?

“Scopes are the specific ____ requested: calendar.events.write, not "full account".”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Scopes are the specific permissions requested: calendar.events.write, not "full account".

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OAuth / OAuth2?

“____ you to Google's /authorize with its client_id, the scope, a redirect_uri, and a PKCE code_challenge.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Client redirects you to Google's /authorize with its client_id, the scope, a redirect_uri, and a PKCE code_challenge.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OAuth / OAuth2?

“An ____ means "can call the API", not "is authenticated now".”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: An access token means "can call the API", not "is authenticated now".

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from OAuth / OAuth2?

“OAuth's core value: the third-party app gets a narrow, revocable token — never your ____, and never more access than the scopes you approved.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: OAuth's core value: the third-party app gets a narrow, revocable token — never your password, and never more access than the scopes you approved.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Sign-On (SSO)?

“Single Sign-On (SSO) lets a user log in once with one ____ provider and then access many separate applications without logging in again to each.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: Single Sign-On (SSO) lets a user log in once with one identity provider and then access many separate applications without logging in again to each.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Sign-On (SSO)?

“OAuth — delegate ____ (API access) to a third-party app.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: OAuth — delegate authorization (API access) to a third-party app.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Sign-On (SSO)?

“It has no session for you, so it redirects your browser to the company IdP with an ____ request.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: It has no session for you, so it redirects your browser to the company IdP with an authentication request.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Sign-On (SSO)?

“It must be highly available with its own ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: It must be highly available with its own redundancy.

system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Sign-On (SSO)?

“SSO centralises authentication: one place to enforce MFA, one place to disable a leaving employee, and far fewer ____ for users to reuse or lose.”
system-design-fundamentals/api-security-.explanation: SSO centralises authentication: one place to enforce MFA, one place to disable a leaving employee, and far fewer passwords for users to reuse or lose.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Synchronous Communication?

“In synchronous ____, the caller sends a request and waits — blocked — until the response comes back before doing anything else.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: In synchronous communication, the caller sends a request and waits — blocked — until the response comes back before doing anything else.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Synchronous Communication?

“Immediate feedback: the caller knows success or ____ right away.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Immediate feedback: the caller knows success or failure right away.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Synchronous Communication?

“____ POST /checkout and stops — the UI shows a spinner.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Client calls POST /checkout and stops — the UI shows a spinner.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Synchronous Communication?

“Without a timeout, one slow ____ can block a caller forever, tying up threads and spreading the slowdown upstream.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Without a timeout, one slow dependency can block a caller forever, tying up threads and spreading the slowdown upstream.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Synchronous Communication?

“____ calls are the right default for anything the user is actively waiting on.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Synchronous calls are the right default for anything the user is actively waiting on.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Communication?

“In asynchronous ____, the caller sends a request and moves on immediately.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: In asynchronous communication, the caller sends a request and moves on immediately.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Communication?

“____: simple, immediate answer, but the caller is blocked and coupled to the callee's speed.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Synchronous: simple, immediate answer, but the caller is blocked and coupled to the callee's speed.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Communication?

“____ the video file to POST /videos.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Client uploads the video file to POST /videos.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Communication?

“"Fire and forget" with no job ID or status ____ leaves users staring at a spinner with no idea if it worked.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: "Fire and forget" with no job ID or status endpoint leaves users staring at a spinner with no idea if it worked.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Communication?

“____ work needs a place to track status (a job record) and a way to notify completion — the extra plumbing is the price of not blocking the user.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Asynchronous work needs a place to track status (a job record) and a way to notify completion — the extra plumbing is the price of not blocking the user.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Request-Response?

“Request-response is the most basic ____ pattern of all: one side sends exactly one request, the other side sends back exactly one response, and the exchange is over.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Request-response is the most basic communication pattern of all: one side sends exactly one request, the other side sends back exactly one response, and the exchange is over.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Request-Response?

“Stateless: the server does not need to remember past requests, so any server can answer any request — great for ____ and scaling.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Stateless: the server does not need to remember past requests, so any server can answer any request — great for load balancing and scaling.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Request-Response?

“Client builds a request: method, URL, headers, optional body — GET /____/42.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Client builds a request: method, URL, headers, optional body — GET /product/42.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Request-Response?

“Calling an endpoint every 200ms to feel "live" wastes ____ compared to a pattern built for pushing updates.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Calling an endpoint every 200ms to feel "live" wastes resources compared to a pattern built for pushing updates.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Request-Response?

“It is the pattern underneath ____ communication, and the starting point every other pattern in this section (polling, streaming, events) modifies or replaces.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: It is the pattern underneath synchronous communication, and the starting point every other pattern in this section (polling, streaming, events) modifies or replaces.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Polling?

“The client is in control: it decides how often to check, and the ____ just answers each check honestly — usually "no, nothing new".”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: The client is in control: it decides how often to check, and the server just answers each check honestly — usually "no, nothing new".

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Polling?

“When updates are frequent or truly need to feel instant, ____, SSE, or WebSockets do better — the later lessons in this section cover each one.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: When updates are frequent or truly need to feel instant, long polling, SSE, or WebSockets do better — the later lessons in this section cover each one.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Polling?

“____ a video-processing job and gets back {jobId: 501, status: "queued"}.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Client submits a video-processing job and gets back {jobId: 501, status: "queued"}.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Polling?

“Every open tab ____ every second multiplies server load fast, mostly for "nothing changed" answers.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Every open tab polling every second multiplies server load fast, mostly for "nothing changed" answers.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Polling?

“That is fine for email, where a minute of delay is invisible — but the server is still answering thousands of "nothing new" ____ a minute from idle users, just in case.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: That is fine for email, where a minute of delay is invisible — but the server is still answering thousands of "nothing new" requests a minute from idle users, just in case.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Long Polling?

“Long polling is regular polling with one twist: instead of answering "nothing new" instantly, the server ____ and only responds once there is something to say — or a timeout is reached.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Long polling is regular polling with one twist: instead of answering "nothing new" instantly, the server holds the request open and only responds once there is something to say — or a timeout is reached.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Long Polling?

“It gets you most of the responsiveness of a real push mechanism, using only plain HTTP request-response — no special ____ needed.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: It gets you most of the responsiveness of a real push mechanism, using only plain HTTP request-response — no special protocol needed.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Long Polling?

“Nothing yet — instead of replying, it ____ and waits.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Nothing yet — instead of replying, it holds the connection open and waits.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Long Polling?

“Without one, dead or forgotten ____ accumulate on the server and eventually exhaust its connection limit.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Without one, dead or forgotten connections accumulate on the server and eventually exhaust its connection limit.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Long Polling?

“That is fine for hundreds, but at huge scale it is exactly the problem ____ and SSE are built to handle more efficiently.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: That is fine for hundreds, but at huge scale it is exactly the problem WebSockets and SSE are built to handle more efficiently.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Server-Sent Events?

“Server-Sent Events (SSE) is one HTTP ____ the client opens once, that the server keeps open and uses to stream a sequence of text messages — one direction only, server to client.”
system-design-fundamentals/communication.explanation: Server-Sent Events (SSE) is one HTTP connection the client opens once, that the server keeps open and uses to stream a sequence of text messages — one direction only, server to client.

system-design-fundamentals/communication.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Server-Sent Events?

“Browsers have this built in via ____ — no library required.”

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.explanation: Caching is keeping a copy of data somewhere faster to reach than its original source, so repeated requests for the same thing are answered quickly instead of redone from scratch.

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Introduction to Caching?

“A ____ means it was not, so you fetch it the slow way and (usually) store it for next time.”
system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.explanation: A cache miss means it was not, so you fetch it the slow way and (usually) store it for next time.

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.prompt:

“GET /bestsellers takes 220 ms, almost all of it one expensive ____ query, and the result barely changes minute to minute.”
system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.explanation: GET /bestsellers takes 220 ms, almost all of it one expensive database query, and the result barely changes minute to minute.

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.explanation: If almost nothing repeats, a cache just adds complexity and memory cost for a hit rate near zero.

system-design-fundamentals/caching--intr.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/caching--appl.explanation: Different servers can answer the same user differently until their local caches happen to agree — confusing, inconsistent behaviour.

system-design-fundamentals/caching--appl.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Application Caching?

system-design-fundamentals/caching--data.explanation: The database's own caching makes individual queries faster.
