system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: On a single machine, function calls are fast and reliable, memory is shared, and there's one clock.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Challenges of Distribution?

“Now that same call goes over a ____ — it can succeed, fail, or hang with no way for the caller to tell "it failed" from "it's just slow."”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Now that same call goes over a network — it can succeed, fail, or hang with no way for the caller to tell "it failed" from "it's just slow."

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Challenges of Distribution?

“Every one of the more specific topics in this section (____, split-brain, heartbeats, failure handling) is really a consequence of taking these challenges seriously instead of assuming them away.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Every one of the more specific topics in this section (partitions, split-brain, heartbeats, failure handling) is really a consequence of taking these challenges seriously instead of assuming them away.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Challenges of Distribution?

“Distributed systems trade a single machine's simplicity for scale and fault tolerance — and that trade means designing deliberately for network unreliability, clock drift, and partial ____ from the start.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Distributed systems trade a single machine's simplicity for scale and fault tolerance — and that trade means designing deliberately for network unreliability, clock drift, and partial failure from the start.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Network Partitions?

“A network ____ happens when a network failure splits a distributed system into two or more groups of machines that can't talk to each other — even though each group is internally healthy and running fine.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: A network partition happens when a network failure splits a distributed system into two or more groups of machines that can't talk to each other — even though each group is internally healthy and running fine.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Network Partitions?

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: The CAP theorem states that during a partition, a system must choose between Consistency (refuse requests that can't be safely answered) and Availability (keep answering, accepting the risk of inconsistency) — it cannot have both at once, because the two halves can't coordinate.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Network Partitions?

“A 6-node cluster split across two data centers replicates writes between all ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: A 6-node cluster split across two data centers replicates writes between all nodes.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Network Partitions?

“Assuming "the ____ is reliable" is one of the classic fallacies of distributed computing — every distributed system will eventually face a partition, so the failure mode needs to be a deliberate design decision, not an afterthought discovered during an actual outage.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Assuming "the network is reliable" is one of the classic fallacies of distributed computing — every distributed system will eventually face a partition, so the failure mode needs to be a deliberate design decision, not an afterthought discovered during an actual outage.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Network Partitions?

“Partitions are a certainty, not a possibility, in any sufficiently large distributed system — the real design question is which guarantee, ____ or availability, you give up when one happens.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Partitions are a certainty, not a possibility, in any sufficiently large distributed system — the real design question is which guarantee, consistency or availability, you give up when one happens.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Split Brain Problem?

“____ is what happens when a network partition causes two halves of a cluster to each believe they are in charge — both accepting writes independently, with no way to know about the other, leading to conflicting, hard-to-reconcile data.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Split brain is what happens when a network partition causes two halves of a cluster to each believe they are in charge — both accepting writes independently, with no way to know about the other, leading to conflicting, hard-to-reconcile data.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Split Brain Problem?

“If a ____ isolates the leader from the rest of the cluster, the other side may (reasonably) elect a new leader, believing the old one is dead.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: If a partition isolates the leader from the rest of the cluster, the other side may (reasonably) elect a new leader, believing the old one is dead.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Split Brain Problem?

“Node 1 is the ____; nodes 2-5 are followers.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Node 1 is the leader; nodes 2-5 are followers.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Split Brain Problem?

“Some systems also add "fencing" (forcibly cutting off a suspected-dead node's access to shared ____) as an extra layer of protection beyond quorum alone.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Some systems also add "fencing" (forcibly cutting off a suspected-dead node's access to shared resources) as an extra layer of protection beyond quorum alone.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Split Brain Problem?

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Split brain happens when a partition lets two sides both believe they're in charge — quorum-based leadership is the standard defense, since only one side of any partition can ever hold a majority.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Heartbeats?

“A heartbeat is a small, periodic "I'm still alive" message one ____ sends to another — the basic mechanism distributed systems use to detect that a peer has failed.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: A heartbeat is a small, periodic "I'm still alive" message one node sends to another — the basic mechanism distributed systems use to detect that a peer has failed.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Heartbeats?

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Heartbeats?

“A node is considered failed if no heartbeat arrives within 6 seconds — a few missed intervals, to absorb normal ____.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: A node is considered failed if no heartbeat arrives within 6 seconds — a few missed intervals, to absorb normal jitter.

system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Heartbeats?

“Setting the timeout too aggressively causes ____ during ordinary network blips or GC pauses, triggering unnecessary failovers.”
system-design-fundamentals/distributed-s.explanation: Setting the timeout too aggressively causes false positives during ordinary network blips or GC pauses, triggering unnecessary failovers.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Metrics give a cheap, continuous, aggregated view of system health — the right tool for "what's happening right now, at scale," with logs and traces stepping in for deeper detail when a metric signals something's wrong.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Alerting & Monitoring?

“____ watches metrics continuously; alerting notifies a human (or triggers an automated response) when something crosses a threshold that indicates a real problem.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Monitoring watches metrics continuously; alerting notifies a human (or triggers an automated response) when something crosses a threshold that indicates a real problem.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Alerting & Monitoring?

“The best alerts are based on ____ users actually experience (elevated error rate, high latency, requests failing) rather than causes (CPU usage, disk space) — a symptom-based alert fires exactly when something is genuinely wrong for users, while a cause-based alert can fire on a perfectly harmless high-CPU period that never actually affects anyone.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: The best alerts are based on symptoms users actually experience (elevated error rate, high latency, requests failing) rather than causes (CPU usage, disk space) — a symptom-based alert fires exactly when something is genuinely wrong for users, while a cause-based alert can fire on a perfectly harmless high-CPU period that never actually affects anyone.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Alerting & Monitoring?

“Cause-based ____ (weaker): "CPU usage exceeded 80%" — might be totally fine (a scheduled batch job), or might not be — the ____ alone can't tell you.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Cause-based alert (weaker): "CPU usage exceeded 80%" — might be totally fine (a scheduled batch job), or might not be — the alert alone can't tell you.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Alerting & Monitoring?

“Over-alerting on noisy, low-signal conditions ____ alert fatigue — engineers start ignoring or muting alerts, including the genuinely important ones, which defeats the entire purpose.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Over-alerting on noisy, low-signal conditions causes alert fatigue — engineers start ignoring or muting alerts, including the genuinely important ones, which defeats the entire purpose.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Alerting & Monitoring?

“Good alerting fires on symptoms users actually feel, with enough context to act on immediately — noisy, cause-based, or context-free ____ erode trust and get ignored.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Good alerting fires on symptoms users actually feel, with enough context to act on immediately — noisy, cause-based, or context-free alerts erode trust and get ignored.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Dashboards & Runbooks?

“A dashboard gives an at-a-glance visual view of a system's key ____; a runbook is a written, step-by-step guide for responding to a specific problem.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: A dashboard gives an at-a-glance visual view of a system's key metrics; a runbook is a written, step-by-step guide for responding to a specific problem.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Dashboards & Runbooks?

“A runbook, linked directly from the corresponding alert, ____ the concrete steps to diagnose and mitigate a specific known failure mode — written in advance, calmly, rather than improvised at 3 AM under pressure.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: A runbook, linked directly from the corresponding alert, documents the concrete steps to diagnose and mitigate a specific known failure mode — written in advance, calmly, rather than improvised at 3 AM under pressure.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Dashboards & Runbooks?

“____ fires: "checkout error rate > 5%," linking directly to both a dashboard and a runbook.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Alert fires: "checkout error rate > 5%," linking directly to both a dashboard and a runbook.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Dashboards & Runbooks?

“Building one giant, cluttered dashboard with every metric ever collected makes finding the signal that actually matters during an incident slower, not faster — purposeful, audience-specific ____ work better than one universal view.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Building one giant, cluttered dashboard with every metric ever collected makes finding the signal that actually matters during an incident slower, not faster — purposeful, audience-specific dashboards work better than one universal view.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Dashboards & Runbooks?

“Dashboards show what's happening; ____ say what to do about it — written and organized in advance, so incident response is fast and guided instead of improvised.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Dashboards show what's happening; runbooks say what to do about it — written and organized in advance, so incident response is fast and guided instead of improvised.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Distributed tracing follows a single request as it travels across every service it touches, recording how long each step took — turning "why was this one request slow" in a microservices architecture from a guessing game into a visual timeline.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:

system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Forgetting to propagate trace context through an asynchronous hop (a message queue, a background job) is another common gap that breaks the trace into disconnected fragments right at that boundary.

system-design-fundamentals/observability.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Distributed Tracing?

“Distributed tracing extends correlation IDs with precise per-hop timing, rendering a request's full path as a visual timeline — the fastest way to find exactly where time went in a multi-____ call.”
system-design-fundamentals/observability.explanation: Distributed tracing extends correlation IDs with precise per-hop timing, rendering a request's full path as a visual timeline — the fastest way to find exactly where time went in a multi-service call.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SSL/TLS?

“TLS (the modern successor to SSL) is what makes HTTPS secure — it encrypts ____ between a client and server, and it verifies the server is actually who it claims to be, both before a single byte of application data is exchanged.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: TLS (the modern successor to SSL) is what makes HTTPS secure — it encrypts traffic between a client and server, and it verifies the server is actually who it claims to be, both before a single byte of application data is exchanged.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SSL/TLS?

“Client and server then use ____ (public/private key pairs) briefly, just to safely agree on a shared secret — ____ is computationally expensive, so it's used only for this initial exchange.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Client and server then use asymmetric encryption (public/private key pairs) briefly, just to safely agree on a shared secret — asymmetric encryption is computationally expensive, so it's used only for this initial exchange.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SSL/TLS?

“____ establishes a shared secret, using asymmetric cryptography briefly for this one exchange.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Handshake establishes a shared secret, using asymmetric cryptography briefly for this one exchange.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SSL/TLS?

“Ignoring ____ expiration monitoring is a surprisingly common cause of real outages — an expired ____ breaks every client's connection the moment it lapses.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Ignoring certificate expiration monitoring is a surprisingly common cause of real outages — an expired certificate breaks every client's connection the moment it lapses.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SSL/TLS?

“TLS combines asymmetric cryptography's ability to establish verified trust with ____'s speed — the handshake proves identity once, then fast encryption protects everything that follows.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: TLS combines asymmetric cryptography's ability to establish verified trust with symmetric encryption's speed — the handshake proves identity once, then fast encryption protects everything that follows.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encryption at Rest?

“____ at rest protects data while it's stored — on disk, in a database, in a backup — so that anyone who gains access to the raw storage medium itself (a stolen drive, an unauthorized cloud storage read) still can't read the data without the ____ key.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data while it's stored — on disk, in a database, in a backup — so that anyone who gains access to the raw storage medium itself (a stolen drive, an unauthorized cloud storage read) still can't read the data without the encryption key.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encryption at Rest?

“Encryption at rest typically works through a ____ that holds the actual encryption keys separately from the encrypted data itself — so that even someone with full access to the storage (the encrypted bytes) still needs a separate, controlled path to the keys to actually decrypt anything.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Encryption at rest typically works through a key management system that holds the actual encryption keys separately from the encrypted data itself — so that even someone with full access to the storage (the encrypted bytes) still needs a separate, controlled path to the keys to actually decrypt anything.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encryption at Rest?

“____ before being written to disk, using a key managed by a separate key management service (KMS) — not stored alongside the data.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Database writes are encrypted before being written to disk, using a key managed by a separate key management service (KMS) — not stored alongside the data.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encryption at Rest?

“Storing encryption keys alongside the data they protect (in the same ____, the same storage bucket) defeats much of the purpose — anyone who accesses the data also gets the key.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Storing encryption keys alongside the data they protect (in the same database, the same storage bucket) defeats much of the purpose — anyone who accesses the data also gets the key.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encryption at Rest?

“Encryption at rest protects stored data from anyone who gains access to the ____ medium itself — but only if the keys are genuinely kept separate, with their own access controls.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Encryption at rest protects stored data from anyone who gains access to the storage medium itself — but only if the keys are genuinely kept separate, with their own access controls.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Secrets Management?

“Secrets management is how a system handles sensitive credentials — API keys, database passwords, ____ keys — safely: never hardcoded, never committed to source control, and issued to services with tight, auditable access control.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Secrets management is how a system handles sensitive credentials — API keys, database passwords, encryption keys — safely: never hardcoded, never committed to source control, and issued to services with tight, auditable access control.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Secrets Management?

“A dedicated secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) stores secrets centrally, encrypted, and hands them out to ____ at runtime through an authenticated API call — instead of secrets being baked into config files, environment variables set by hand, or worst of all, committed directly into source code.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: A dedicated secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) stores secrets centrally, encrypted, and hands them out to services at runtime through an authenticated API call — instead of secrets being baked into config files, environment variables set by hand, or worst of all, committed directly into source code.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Secrets Management?

“Instead of it being hardcoded, the service authenticates to the secrets manager at startup and ____ it.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Instead of it being hardcoded, the service authenticates to the secrets manager at startup and requests it.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Secrets Management?

“Granting overly broad access (every ____ can read every secret) also defeats much of the value — access should be scoped to exactly what each ____ actually needs.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Granting overly broad access (every service can read every secret) also defeats much of the value — access should be scoped to exactly what each service actually needs.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Secrets Management?

“Centralized, audited ____ management replaces hardcoded credentials with authenticated, revocable, rotatable access — turning a leaked secret from a catastrophe into a manageable, logged event.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Centralized, audited secrets management replaces hardcoded credentials with authenticated, revocable, rotatable access — turning a leaked secret from a catastrophe into a manageable, logged event.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Password Management?

“Password management is how a system stores user ____ so that even if the database is stolen, attackers can't easily recover the original ____ — the core technique is hashing, done specifically so it's slow.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Password management is how a system stores user passwords so that even if the database is stolen, attackers can't easily recover the original passwords — the core technique is hashing, done specifically so it's slow.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Password Management?

“A ____ is never stored directly — only its hash is stored, and a login check re-hashes the entered ____ and compares hashes.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: A password is never stored directly — only its hash is stored, and a login check re-hashes the entered password and compares hashes.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Password Management?

“A ____ random salt is generated for this user.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: A unique random salt is generated for this user.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Password Management?

“Skipping a unique salt per user, or reusing one global salt, ____ the system vulnerable to precomputed rainbow-table attacks across the whole user base at once.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Skipping a unique salt per user, or reusing one global salt, leaves the system vulnerable to precomputed rainbow-table attacks across the whole user base at once.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Password Management?

“Password security comes from hashing that's deliberately slow, combined with a unique salt per user — making large-scale guessing attacks impractical even if the password ____ is stolen.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Password security comes from hashing that's deliberately slow, combined with a unique salt per user — making large-scale guessing attacks impractical even if the password database is stolen.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from RBAC?

“Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) grants ____ to roles rather than to individual users directly, then assigns users to roles — making access control manageable at scale instead of tracking ____ per person.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) grants permissions to roles rather than to individual users directly, then assigns users to roles — making access control manageable at scale instead of tracking permissions per person.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from RBAC?

“With RBAC, permissions are defined once per role (like "editor" or "admin"), and a user's access comes entirely from whichever ____ they're assigned.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: With RBAC, permissions are defined once per role (like "editor" or "admin"), and a user's access comes entirely from whichever roles they're assigned.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from RBAC?

“Define roles. "Viewer" can read ____; "Editor" can read and write; "Admin" can read, write, and manage users.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Define roles. "Viewer" can read documents; "Editor" can read and write; "Admin" can read, write, and manage users.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from RBAC?

“"Role explosion" — creating an ever-growing number of hyper-specific roles for every slight permission variation — eventually recreates the same unmanageable complexity ____ was meant to solve.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: "Role explosion" — creating an ever-growing number of hyper-specific roles for every slight permission variation — eventually recreates the same unmanageable complexity RBAC was meant to solve.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from RBAC?

“RBAC makes access control manageable at organizational scale by attaching permissions to roles rather than individuals — the trick is keeping the ____ set itself small and meaningful.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: RBAC makes access control manageable at organizational scale by attaching permissions to roles rather than individuals — the trick is keeping the role set itself small and meaningful.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SAML?

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is a standard that lets a user log in once with an identity provider (like their company's Okta or Azure AD) and be securely recognized by many different applications — the backbone of enterprise single sign-on (SSO).

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SAML?

“SAML involves three parties: the user, the ____ — who actually verifies who the user is — and the service provider (SP) — the application the user wants to use.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: SAML involves three parties: the user, the identity provider (IdP) — who actually verifies who the user is — and the service provider (SP) — the application the user wants to use.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SAML?

“____ (the SP) and isn't logged in yet.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: User opens a work application (the SP) and isn't logged in yet.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SAML?

“Failing to properly verify a SAML assertion's digital ____ is a critical vulnerability — it's exactly what stops an attacker from forging their own fake assertion claiming to be someone else.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: Failing to properly verify a SAML assertion's digital signature is a critical vulnerability — it's exactly what stops an attacker from forging their own fake assertion claiming to be someone else.

system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SAML?

“SAML lets one trusted identity provider vouch for a user's identity to many applications via signed assertions — centralizing ____ so individual applications never handle passwords directly.”
system-design-fundamentals/advanced-secu.explanation: SAML lets one trusted identity provider vouch for a user's identity to many applications via signed assertions — centralizing authentication so individual applications never handle passwords directly.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--what-.explanation: HLD is theory applied to one specific system, stopping at the boundary of components and their contracts — one level more concrete than Fundamentals, one level less detailed than LLD.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Requirements Clarification?

“Every HLD prompt is deliberately under-specified — “____ Twitter” could mean a dozen different systems, and the first real skill is narrowing it down before designing anything.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.explanation: Every HLD prompt is deliberately under-specified — “design Twitter” could mean a dozen different systems, and the first real skill is narrowing it down before designing anything.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Requirements Clarification?

“____ are the qualities the system must have while doing so — scale, latency, availability, consistency needs.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.explanation: Non-functional requirements are the qualities the system must have while doing so — scale, latency, availability, consistency needs.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Requirements Clarification?

“____ the narrowed scope back. “So we’re designing posting, following, and an eventually-consistent timeline for 50M users” — now there’s something concrete to design.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.explanation: State the narrowed scope back. “So we’re designing posting, following, and an eventually-consistent timeline for 50M users” — now there’s something concrete to design.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Requirements Clarification?

“Silently assuming scope (deciding internally that likes are out of scope without saying so) ____ the person listening unsure what’s actually being designed.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.explanation: Silently assuming scope (deciding internally that likes are out of scope without saying so) leaves the person listening unsure what’s actually being designed.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Requirements Clarification?

“Clarifying ____ isn’t a formality before the real work starts — it is the first piece of real design work, since it determines what “done” even means.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--requi.explanation: Clarifying requirements isn’t a formality before the real work starts — it is the first piece of real design work, since it determines what “done” even means.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.prompt: What is the main purpose of capacity estimation?
options: Choose an appropriate order of magnitude for the design
high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.explanation: Rough estimates identify which resources and architecture choices the workload actually needs.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.prompt: 100 million new URLs are created in a 30-day month. Approximately how many writes per second is that?
high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.explanation: 100,000,000 ÷ (30 × 86,400) is about 38.6, or roughly 40 writes per second.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.prompt: At 40 writes per second and a 100:1 read-to-write ratio, what is the read rate?
high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.explanation: Multiply 40 by 100 to estimate 4,000 reads per second.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.prompt: 1.2 billion records at roughly 500 bytes each require how much raw storage?
high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.explanation: 1.2 billion × 500 bytes = 600 billion bytes, approximately 600 GB before overhead and replicas.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.prompt: The workload has far more reads than writes and repeatedly accesses popular URLs. Which change is most directly supported?
options: Add a cache for popular URL mappings
Serialize every read through one global lock
high-level-design/hld-foundations--capac.explanation: Caching reduces repeated read traffic. The estimated write and storage volumes alone do not justify sharding.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Defining APIs and Data Models?

“Once ____ and scale are clear, the next step is writing down a small set of APIs and a first-draft data model — the contract every component in the design will be built against.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.explanation: Once requirements and scale are clear, the next step is writing down a small set of APIs and a first-draft data model — the contract every component in the design will be built against.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Defining APIs and Data Models?

“APIs at this stage should be ____ — a handful of endpoints matching the functional requirements, not a method for every internal operation.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.explanation: APIs at this stage should be coarse-grained and resource-oriented — a handful of endpoints matching the functional requirements, not a method for every internal operation.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Defining APIs and Data Models?

“A ____ shortener needs to create a short ____ and resolve one back to its original.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.explanation: A URL shortener needs to create a short URL and resolve one back to its original.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Defining APIs and Data Models?

“Designing APIs around internal ____ details (a separate endpoint for every database column update) creates a leaky, brittle contract.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.explanation: Designing APIs around internal implementation details (a separate endpoint for every database column update) creates a leaky, brittle contract.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Defining APIs and Data Models?

“A small, resource-oriented API surface and a first-draft data model turn requirements into a concrete ____ — the thing every later component in the design gets built against.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--defin.explanation: A small, resource-oriented API surface and a first-draft data model turn requirements into a concrete contract — the thing every later component in the design gets built against.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Identifying Core Components?

“With APIs and a data model in hand, the last foundational step is drawing the actual boxes — deciding what’s a separate service, what’s a ____, and what supporting pieces the capacity estimate has already justified.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.explanation: With APIs and a data model in hand, the last foundational step is drawing the actual boxes — deciding what’s a separate service, what’s a datastore, and what supporting pieces the capacity estimate has already justified.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Identifying Core Components?

“A component earns its own box when it has a distinct ____, can scale or fail independently, or was specifically justified by the capacity estimate (a cache because reads dominate, a queue because writes need to be smoothed out).”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.explanation: A component earns its own box when it has a distinct responsibility, can scale or fail independently, or was specifically justified by the capacity estimate (a cache because reads dominate, a queue because writes need to be smoothed out).

high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Identifying Core Components?

“Start from the API ____ and data model already defined — that’s always the first box.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.explanation: Start from the API service and data model already defined — that’s always the first box.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Identifying Core Components?

“Adding components by default — a ____, a search index, a separate microservice per entity — because they “seem like good practice” produces an over-engineered design that can’t be justified when questioned.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.explanation: Adding components by default — a message queue, a search index, a separate microservice per entity — because they “seem like good practice” produces an over-engineered design that can’t be justified when questioned.

high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Identifying Core Components?

“Every box on the diagram should trace back to a stated requirement or a specific number from the ____ — that traceability is what makes a design defensible rather than just familiar-looking.”
high-level-design/hld-foundations--ident.explanation: Every box on the diagram should trace back to a stated requirement or a specific number from the estimate — that traceability is what makes a design defensible rather than just familiar-looking.

high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Horizontal and Vertical Scaling?

“When a ____ outgrows one machine, there are exactly two directions to go: make that one machine bigger (vertical), or add more machines that share the load (horizontal).”
high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.explanation: When a design outgrows one machine, there are exactly two directions to go: make that one machine bigger (vertical), or add more machines that share the load (horizontal).

high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Horizontal and Vertical Scaling?

“It’s simple (no code changes, no coordination between nodes) but hits a hard ceiling and creates a ____.”
high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.explanation: It’s simple (no code changes, no coordination between nodes) but hits a hard ceiling and creates a single point of failure.

high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Horizontal and Vertical Scaling?

“That’s well within a single well-specified server’s capacity — ____ (a bigger box) is the simplest correct answer for now.”
high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.explanation: That’s well within a single well-specified server’s capacity — vertical scaling (a bigger box) is the simplest correct answer for now.

high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Horizontal and Vertical Scaling?

“Reaching for ____ by default, even when the estimate shows a single well-sized machine would comfortably handle the load, adds coordination complexity (load balancing, statelessness, distributed state) for no real benefit.”
high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.explanation: Reaching for horizontal scaling by default, even when the estimate shows a single well-sized machine would comfortably handle the load, adds coordination complexity (load balancing, statelessness, distributed state) for no real benefit.

high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Horizontal and Vertical Scaling?

“Start with the simplest option the ____ actually justifies — vertical scaling first, horizontal scaling once a single machine genuinely can’t keep up.”
high-level-design/scalability--horizonta.explanation: Start with the simplest option the estimate actually justifies — vertical scaling first, horizontal scaling once a single machine genuinely can’t keep up.

high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing?

“In an HLD diagram, it’s the box that appears the instant ____ shows up.”
high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.explanation: In an HLD diagram, it’s the box that appears the instant horizontal scaling shows up.

high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing?

“A ____ sits between clients and a fleet of identical service instances, distributing requests across them (round robin, least-connections, or by a consistent hash of the request).”
high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.explanation: A load balancer sits between clients and a fleet of identical service instances, distributing requests across them (round robin, least-connections, or by a consistent hash of the request).

high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing?

“Three identical API ____ instances are deployed to share the load.”
high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.explanation: Three identical API service instances are deployed to share the load.

high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing?

“Forgetting that the load balancer itself can become a ____ is a common oversight — production designs run at least two load balancer instances behind a shared virtual IP or DNS.”
high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.explanation: Forgetting that the load balancer itself can become a single point of failure is a common oversight — production designs run at least two load balancer instances behind a shared virtual IP or DNS.

high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Load Balancing?

“A load balancer is what makes a fleet of instances behave like one reliable service to the outside world — but it needs the same ____ thinking applied to everything behind it.”
high-level-design/scalability--load-bala.explanation: A load balancer is what makes a fleet of instances behave like one reliable service to the outside world — but it needs the same redundancy thinking applied to everything behind it.

high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Caching Strategy?

“Whenever an estimate shows reads far outnumbering writes, a cache is usually the single highest-leverage box you can add to a design — it absorbs the read traffic before it ever reaches the ____.”
high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.explanation: Whenever an estimate shows reads far outnumbering writes, a cache is usually the single highest-leverage box you can add to a design — it absorbs the read traffic before it ever reaches the database.

high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Caching Strategy?

“A cache stores the results of expensive reads in fast, usually in-memory ____ (Redis, Memcached).”
high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.explanation: A cache stores the results of expensive reads in fast, usually in-memory storage (Redis, Memcached).

high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Caching Strategy?

“____ shows 4,000 reads/sec against 40 writes/sec for URL redirects — a strong signal to cache.”
high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.explanation: Estimate shows 4,000 reads/sec against 40 writes/sec for URL redirects — a strong signal to cache.

high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Caching Strategy?

“Forgetting an invalidation ____ entirely is worse — a cache that never expires stale data quietly serves wrong answers indefinitely.”
high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.explanation: Forgetting an invalidation strategy entirely is worse — a cache that never expires stale data quietly serves wrong answers indefinitely.

high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Caching Strategy?

“A cache is the highest-leverage box for ____ designs, but it’s only as good as its invalidation strategy — the database still has to remain the source of truth.”
high-level-design/scalability--caching-s.explanation: A cache is the highest-leverage box for read-heavy designs, but it’s only as good as its invalidation strategy — the database still has to remain the source of truth.

high-level-design/scalability--content-d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“A CDN pushes static or slow-changing content physically closer to users around the world — it’s the box you add the moment a ____ serves images, video, or any asset to a geographically spread-out audience.”
high-level-design/scalability--content-d.explanation: A CDN pushes static or slow-changing content physically closer to users around the world — it’s the box you add the moment a design serves images, video, or any asset to a geographically spread-out audience.

high-level-design/scalability--content-d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“It reduces both latency (physical distance) and origin load (most ____ never reach the origin at all).”
high-level-design/scalability--content-d.explanation: It reduces both latency (physical distance) and origin load (most requests never reach the origin at all).

high-level-design/scalability--content-d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“____ to users worldwide from a single origin data center.”
high-level-design/scalability--content-d.explanation: A video platform serves thumbnails to users worldwide from a single origin data center.

high-level-design/scalability--content-d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“Forgetting a CDN entirely for a globally-distributed, asset-heavy design (images, video, downloads) ____ an easy, high-impact optimization on the table.”
high-level-design/scalability--content-d.explanation: Forgetting a CDN entirely for a globally-distributed, asset-heavy design (images, video, downloads) leaves an easy, high-impact optimization on the table.

high-level-design/scalability--content-d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Content Delivery Networks?

“A CDN is the answer specifically to “users are far from my origin server” for static or slow-changing content — it belongs on the ____ whenever both of those are true.”
high-level-design/scalability--content-d.explanation: A CDN is the answer specifically to “users are far from my origin server” for static or slow-changing content — it belongs on the diagram whenever both of those are true.

high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Processing?

“Not every piece of work a request triggers needs to finish before the user gets a response — ____ processing moves the slow, non-urgent parts off the request path entirely.”
high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.explanation: Not every piece of work a request triggers needs to finish before the user gets a response — asynchronous processing moves the slow, non-urgent parts off the request path entirely.

high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Processing?

“This keeps request ____ low and lets the queue absorb bursts of load that would otherwise overwhelm downstream systems.”
high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.explanation: This keeps request latency low and lets the queue absorb bursts of load that would otherwise overwhelm downstream systems.

high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Processing?

“The upload itself must be ____ — the user is waiting for confirmation it succeeded.”
high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.explanation: The upload itself must be synchronous — the user is waiting for confirmation it succeeded.

high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Processing?

“When a request does something that’s slow but doesn’t need to complete before responding (sending a confirmation email, generating a video thumbnail, recording an analytics event), the API ____ can hand that work to a queue and respond to the user immediately.”
high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.explanation: When a request does something that’s slow but doesn’t need to complete before responding (sending a confirmation email, generating a video thumbnail, recording an analytics event), the API service can hand that work to a queue and respond to the user immediately.

high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Asynchronous Processing?

“Ask, for every piece of work a request triggers, whether the user is actually waiting on it — if not, a ____ and a background worker keep it off the critical path.”
high-level-design/scalability--asynchron.explanation: Ask, for every piece of work a request triggers, whether the user is actually waiting on it — if not, a queue and a background worker keep it off the critical path.

high-level-design/scalability--performan.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Performance Bottlenecks?

“A system is only ever as fast as its single slowest dependency on the critical path — finding that one ____ matters far more than optimizing everything else around it.”
high-level-design/scalability--performan.explanation: A system is only ever as fast as its single slowest dependency on the critical path — finding that one bottleneck matters far more than optimizing everything else around it.

high-level-design/scalability--performan.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Performance Bottlenecks?

“A bottleneck is the component that limits overall ____ or latency even when every other component has spare capacity.”
high-level-design/scalability--performan.explanation: A bottleneck is the component that limits overall throughput or latency even when every other component has spare capacity.

high-level-design/scalability--performan.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Performance Bottlenecks?

“API ____ is scaled to 20 instances, but overall throughput hasn’t improved as expected.”
high-level-design/scalability--performan.explanation: API service is scaled to 20 instances, but overall throughput hasn’t improved as expected.

high-level-design/scalability--performan.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Performance Bottlenecks?

“Scaling out a layer that already has spare ____, without first tracing where time is actually spent, wastes effort and cost while the real bottleneck stays untouched.”
high-level-design/scalability--performan.explanation: Scaling out a layer that already has spare capacity, without first tracing where time is actually spent, wastes effort and cost while the real bottleneck stays untouched.

high-level-design/scalability--performan.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Performance Bottlenecks?

“Find the single slowest ____ on the critical path before optimizing anything else — every other improvement is wasted until that one bottleneck is addressed.”
high-level-design/scalability--performan.explanation: Find the single slowest dependency on the critical path before optimizing anything else — every other improvement is wasted until that one bottleneck is addressed.

high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Choosing a Database?

“The ____ choice should fall out of the data model and access patterns already defined earlier in the design — not be picked first out of familiarity or trend.”
high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.explanation: The database choice should fall out of the data model and access patterns already defined earlier in the design — not be picked first out of familiarity or trend.

high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Choosing a Database?

“Three questions narrow the choice fast: how ____ is the data (many joins across entities favor a relational database), how flexible does the schema need to be (rapidly-changing or sparse fields favor a document store), and what access pattern dominates (simple key lookups at huge scale favor a key-value store; full-text search favors a search index).”
high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.explanation: Three questions narrow the choice fast: how structured and relational is the data (many joins across entities favor a relational database), how flexible does the schema need to be (rapidly-changing or sparse fields favor a document store), and what access pattern dominates (simple key lookups at huge scale favor a key-value store; full-text search favors a search index).

high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Choosing a Database?

“____ needs orders, line items, and customers, with joins between them and strict correctness on totals — a relational database fits well.”
high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.explanation: An orders system needs orders, line items, and customers, with joins between them and strict correctness on totals — a relational database fits well.

high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Choosing a Database?

“Forcing every ____ through one datastore “to keep things simple” frequently produces worse performance than a small number of purpose-fit stores would.”
high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.explanation: Forcing every access pattern through one datastore “to keep things simple” frequently produces worse performance than a small number of purpose-fit stores would.

high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Choosing a Database?

“Let the data model and access patterns choose the database, not the other way around — and expect a non-trivial ____ to use more than one kind of store.”
high-level-design/data-layer--choosing-a.explanation: Let the data model and access patterns choose the database, not the other way around — and expect a non-trivial design to use more than one kind of store.

high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SQL vs NoSQL?

““SQL or NoSQL” isn’t really one decision — it’s shorthand for a handful of narrower trade-offs around ____, schema flexibility, and how the data will scale.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.explanation: “SQL or NoSQL” isn’t really one decision — it’s shorthand for a handful of narrower trade-offs around consistency, schema flexibility, and how the data will scale.

high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SQL vs NoSQL?

“Relational (SQL) databases give strong consistency, ____ across multiple rows and tables, and a fixed schema that catches structural mistakes early — well suited to data where correctness and relationships matter (money, inventory, anything with joins).”
high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.explanation: Relational (SQL) databases give strong consistency, transactions across multiple rows and tables, and a fixed schema that catches structural mistakes early — well suited to data where correctness and relationships matter (money, inventory, anything with joins).

high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SQL vs NoSQL?

“Debits and credits must balance exactly, across multiple rows, inside one ____ — a relational database’s guarantees are exactly what this needs.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.explanation: Debits and credits must balance exactly, across multiple rows, inside one transaction — a relational database’s guarantees are exactly what this needs.

high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SQL vs NoSQL?

“Treating this as one binary choice for the entire system, rather than a per-entity decision, forces a compromise somewhere — either awkward transactions bolted onto a NoSQL store, or a ____ schema stretched to hold loosely-structured data it wasn’t designed for.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.explanation: Treating this as one binary choice for the entire system, rather than a per-entity decision, forces a compromise somewhere — either awkward transactions bolted onto a NoSQL store, or a relational schema stretched to hold loosely-structured data it wasn’t designed for.

high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from SQL vs NoSQL?

“Ask the SQL-vs-NoSQL question per entity, driven by whether that entity needs strong cross-row consistency or benefits more from flexible ____ and easier horizontal scale.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sql-vs-nos.explanation: Ask the SQL-vs-NoSQL question per entity, driven by whether that entity needs strong cross-row consistency or benefits more from flexible schema and easier horizontal scale.

high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Replication?

“____ keeps copies of the same data on multiple machines — the standard answer to “what happens if the database server dies” and, often, to read scaling as well.”
high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.explanation: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple machines — the standard answer to “what happens if the database server dies” and, often, to read scaling as well.

high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Replication?

“A ____ setup sends all writes to one primary, which streams changes to one or more replicas that serve read traffic.”
high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.explanation: A primary-replica setup sends all writes to one primary, which streams changes to one or more replicas that serve read traffic.

high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Replication?

“____ against a single database instance already near its limit.”
high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.explanation: Estimate shows heavy read traffic against a single database instance already near its limit.

high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Replication?

“Assuming replica promotion is instant and lossless is another common gap; ____ takes real time and can lose the last few unreplicated writes.”
high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.explanation: Assuming replica promotion is instant and lossless is another common gap; failover takes real time and can lose the last few unreplicated writes.

high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Replication?

“Replication buys read scale and failover protection at the cost of ____ — design around that lag explicitly rather than assuming replicas are always perfectly up to date.”
high-level-design/data-layer--replicatio.explanation: Replication buys read scale and failover protection at the cost of replication lag — design around that lag explicitly rather than assuming replicas are always perfectly up to date.

high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Sharding?

“When a dataset outgrows what any single machine can hold or serve — even with replicas — ____ splits it across multiple independent databases, each holding a slice of the data.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.explanation: When a dataset outgrows what any single machine can hold or serve — even with replicas — sharding splits it across multiple independent databases, each holding a slice of the data.

high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Sharding?

“Unlike ____ — where every replica holds the same full data — each shard holds only its own slice, so total capacity scales with the number of shards.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.explanation: Unlike replication — where every replica holds the same full data — each shard holds only its own slice, so total capacity scales with the number of shards.

high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Sharding?

“A single database can no longer hold the full user dataset, even with ____ absorbing read traffic.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.explanation: A single database can no longer hold the full user dataset, even with read replicas absorbing read traffic.

high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Sharding?

“Choosing a ____ that doesn’t match how data is actually queried is the other classic mistake — it turns nearly every query into an expensive fan-out across all shards, defeating the purpose.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.explanation: Choosing a shard key that doesn’t match how data is actually queried is the other classic mistake — it turns nearly every query into an expensive fan-out across all shards, defeating the purpose.

high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Sharding?

“Shard only once the data or load genuinely exceeds one machine’s ____, and choose the shard key to match the query pattern the design actually needs to serve fast.”
high-level-design/data-layer--sharding.explanation: Shard only once the data or load genuinely exceeds one machine’s capacity, and choose the shard key to match the query pattern the design actually needs to serve fast.

high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Partitioning?

“____ splits a large table into smaller, more manageable pieces — and unlike sharding, it can often be done inside a single database, with no extra machines involved.”
high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.explanation: Partitioning splits a large table into smaller, more manageable pieces — and unlike sharding, it can often be done inside a single database, with no extra machines involved.

high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Partitioning?

“A common form is ____: splitting a table by a value range, most often time (one partition per month, say).”
high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.explanation: A common form is range partitioning: splitting a table by a value range, most often time (one partition per month, say).

high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Partitioning?

“An ____ table grows by millions of rows a day, and queries for “last week’s ____” are getting slower as the table grows.”
high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.explanation: An events table grows by millions of rows a day, and queries for “last week’s events” are getting slower as the table grows.

high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Partitioning?

“Confusing partitioning with sharding leads to reaching for the wrong tool — partitioning solves “one table is too big” within one database, while sharding solves “the whole dataset is too big for one database.” Choosing a ____ key that doesn’t match the dominant query pattern (partitioning by user ID when almost every query filters by date) gives up most of the benefit.”
high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.explanation: Confusing partitioning with sharding leads to reaching for the wrong tool — partitioning solves “one table is too big” within one database, while sharding solves “the whole dataset is too big for one database.” Choosing a partition key that doesn’t match the dominant query pattern (partitioning by user ID when almost every query filters by date) gives up most of the benefit.

high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Partitioning?

“Partitioning is the lighter-weight lever — reach for it when one table has grown unwieldy, before reaching for ____’s added operational complexity.”
high-level-design/data-layer--partitioni.explanation: Partitioning is the lighter-weight lever — reach for it when one table has grown unwieldy, before reaching for sharding’s added operational complexity.

high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Consistency?

“Once data lives in more than one place — a ____, a cache, a second data center — the design has to decide, deliberately, how quickly those copies are allowed to agree.”
high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.explanation: Once data lives in more than one place — a replica, a cache, a second data center — the design has to decide, deliberately, how quickly those copies are allowed to agree.

high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Consistency?

“____ allows a brief window where different copies disagree, in exchange for lower latency and higher availability.”
high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.explanation: Eventual consistency allows a brief window where different copies disagree, in exchange for lower latency and higher availability.

high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Consistency?

“Showing a like count that’s a few seconds stale has essentially no real consequence — not worth paying strong-____ latency for.”
high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.explanation: Showing a like count that’s a few seconds stale has essentially no real consequence — not worth paying strong-consistency latency for.

high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Consistency?

“Defaulting an entire system to ____ “to be safe” pays a latency and availability cost everywhere, even where it isn’t needed.”
high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.explanation: Defaulting an entire system to strong consistency “to be safe” pays a latency and availability cost everywhere, even where it isn’t needed.

high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Data Consistency?

“Consistency is a per-data-type ____ decision, not a single system-wide setting — spend strong consistency’s cost only where being wrong is actually expensive.”
high-level-design/data-layer--data-consi.explanation: Consistency is a per-data-type design decision, not a single system-wide setting — spend strong consistency’s cost only where being wrong is actually expensive.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“CAP theorem is the reminder that once a system is split across a network that can fail, you cannot have perfect consistency and perfect ____ at the same time — and every HLD design implicitly picks a side.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: CAP theorem is the reminder that once a system is split across a network that can fail, you cannot have perfect consistency and perfect availability at the same time — and every HLD design implicitly picks a side.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“CAP says a distributed system, during a ____, must choose between consistency (every node sees the same data, but some requests may be refused) and availability (every request gets a response, but it might be stale).”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: CAP says a distributed system, during a network partition, must choose between consistency (every node sees the same data, but some requests may be refused) and availability (every request gets a response, but it might be stale).

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“Selling the last unit of stock twice is a real business problem — during a ____, better to refuse the sale than risk overselling.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Selling the last unit of stock twice is a real business problem — during a partition, better to refuse the sale than risk overselling.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“Forgetting that CAP only applies during an actual partition — and that most of the time, a well-designed system gives both ____ and availability — leads to over-engineering for a rare event.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Forgetting that CAP only applies during an actual partition — and that most of the time, a well-designed system gives both consistency and availability — leads to over-engineering for a rare event.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from CAP Theorem?

“Use CAP as a prompt to ____, out loud, which side each piece of data falls on during a partition — not as a single label for the whole system.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Use CAP as a prompt to state, out loud, which side each piece of data falls on during a partition — not as a single label for the whole system.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“Whenever a design distributes data or requests across a changing set of nodes — shards, cache servers — ____ is what keeps adding or removing one node from reshuffling everything else.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Whenever a design distributes data or requests across a changing set of nodes — shards, cache servers — consistent hashing is what keeps adding or removing one node from reshuffling everything else.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“With naive ____ ( hash(key) % N ), changing N — adding or removing one node — remaps almost every key to a different node.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: With naive hashing ( hash(key) % N ), changing N — adding or removing one node — remaps almost every key to a different node.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“____ sit on a hash ring, each owning the keys between itself and the next server clockwise.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Three cache servers sit on a hash ring, each owning the keys between itself and the next server clockwise.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“Placing too few points per node on the ring can also create uneven load, which is why real implementations typically use multiple “____” per physical node to smooth the distribution.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Placing too few points per node on the ring can also create uneven load, which is why real implementations typically use multiple “virtual nodes” per physical node to smooth the distribution.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Consistent Hashing?

“Consistent hashing is the specific tool that makes a distributed ____ or shard fleet elastic — safe to grow or shrink without reshuffling data that didn’t need to move.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--c.explanation: Consistent hashing is the specific tool that makes a distributed cache or shard fleet elastic — safe to grow or shrink without reshuffling data that didn’t need to move.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Leader Election?

“Whenever a design needs exactly one node to make a decision — who’s the primary database, who assigns work — a ____ mechanism is what the group of nodes uses to agree on who that one node is.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.explanation: Whenever a design needs exactly one node to make a decision — who’s the primary database, who assigns work — a leader election mechanism is what the group of nodes uses to agree on who that one node is.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Leader Election?

“Leader election lets a group of nodes agree on a single leader, and — critically — detect and replace that leader if it fails, without any node needing to be manually configured as “the one.” Nodes typically exchange ____; if the leader stops heartbeating, the remaining nodes run an election (often via an underlying consensus protocol) to pick a new one.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.explanation: Leader election lets a group of nodes agree on a single leader, and — critically — detect and replace that leader if it fails, without any node needing to be manually configured as “the one.” Nodes typically exchange heartbeats; if the leader stops heartbeating, the remaining nodes run an election (often via an underlying consensus protocol) to pick a new one.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Leader Election?

“____ run a leader election protocol on startup; one becomes the primary, the other two become replicas.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.explanation: Three database nodes run a leader election protocol on startup; one becomes the primary, the other two become replicas.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Leader Election?

“A subtler failure mode, ____ — two nodes each believing they’re the leader after a partition — is why real implementations require a majority of nodes to agree before an election succeeds.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.explanation: A subtler failure mode, split brain — two nodes each believing they’re the leader after a partition — is why real implementations require a majority of nodes to agree before an election succeeds.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Leader Election?

“____ election turns “who’s in charge” from a manual, human-driven decision into something the system detects and resolves automatically when a ____ fails.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--l.explanation: Leader election turns “who’s in charge” from a manual, human-driven decision into something the system detects and resolves automatically when a leader fails.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Distributed Locks?

“When two processes on different machines might otherwise act on the same resource at the same time, a distributed lock is what makes sure only one of them proceeds — a single-machine mutex extended across the ____.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.explanation: When two processes on different machines might otherwise act on the same resource at the same time, a distributed lock is what makes sure only one of them proceeds — a single-machine mutex extended across the network.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Distributed Locks?

“Because a process holding the lock can crash without releasing it, locks are given a ____ so they expire automatically — trading a small risk of the lock expiring too early against the much larger risk of a permanently stuck resource.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.explanation: Because a process holding the lock can crash without releasing it, locks are given a time-to-live so they expire automatically — trading a small risk of the lock expiring too early against the much larger risk of a permanently stuck resource.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Distributed Locks?

“____ must run on exactly one instance, even though the job scheduler runs on every instance of the service.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.explanation: A nightly billing job must run on exactly one instance, even though the job scheduler runs on every instance of the service.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Distributed Locks?

“Forgetting a TTL on the ____ means a crashed process holds it forever, permanently blocking the resource.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.explanation: Forgetting a TTL on the lock means a crashed process holds it forever, permanently blocking the resource.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Distributed Locks?

“A distributed lock ____ access across machines the way a mutex does on one — with the added, unavoidable wrinkle of needing an expiry for when the lock holder disappears.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--d.explanation: A distributed lock coordinates access across machines the way a mutex does on one — with the added, unavoidable wrinkle of needing an expiry for when the lock holder disappears.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Message Queues?

“A ____ sits between a producer and a consumer, holding work until the consumer is ready for it — the component that turns a fragile direct call into something that survives the receiving side being slow, overloaded, or briefly down.”
