high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.explanation: A message queue sits between a producer and a consumer, holding work until the consumer is ready for it — the component that turns a fragile direct call into something that survives the receiving side being slow, overloaded, or briefly down.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Message Queues?

“This ____ the two sides in time (the consumer doesn’t need to be up right now) and in load (a traffic spike piles up in the queue instead of overwhelming the consumer directly).”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.explanation: This decouples the two sides in time (the consumer doesn’t need to be up right now) and in load (a traffic spike piles up in the queue instead of overwhelming the consumer directly).

high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Message Queues?

“The order ____ publishes one “order placed” message to a queue and returns to the user immediately.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.explanation: The order service publishes one “order placed” message to a queue and returns to the user immediately.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Message Queues?

“Assuming a ____ will only ever see a message once, without handling duplicate delivery, is the other common gap — most queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.explanation: Assuming a consumer will only ever see a message once, without handling duplicate delivery, is the other common gap — most queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Message Queues?

“A message ____ decouples producers from consumers in both time and load — the default answer whenever downstream work doesn’t need to finish before responding to the original request.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--m.explanation: A message queue decouples producers from consumers in both time and load — the default answer whenever downstream work doesn’t need to finish before responding to the original request.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Event Streaming?

“Event streaming extends the ____ idea from “deliver this once and forget it” to “keep an ordered, replayable log that many independent consumers can each read at their own pace.””
high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.explanation: Event streaming extends the message queue idea from “deliver this once and forget it” to “keep an ordered, replayable log that many independent consumers can each read at their own pace.”

high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Event Streaming?

“This makes it a natural fit when the same events need to feed several different systems — analytics, search indexing, ____ — each reading independently, and when new consumers need to be able to replay history.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.explanation: This makes it a natural fit when the same events need to feed several different systems — analytics, search indexing, notifications — each reading independently, and when new consumers need to be able to replay history.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Event Streaming?

“Every “order placed” event is written to an orders ____, in the order it happened.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.explanation: Every “order placed” event is written to an orders stream, in the order it happened.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Event Streaming?

“Forgetting that ordering is typically only guaranteed within one ____ of the stream, not across the whole stream, can also produce subtle ordering bugs at scale.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.explanation: Forgetting that ordering is typically only guaranteed within one partition of the stream, not across the whole stream, can also produce subtle ordering bugs at scale.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Event Streaming?

“Reach for a stream over a plain queue specifically when several independent consumers need the same ____, or when replaying history is a real requirement — not by default.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--e.explanation: Reach for a stream over a plain queue specifically when several independent consumers need the same events, or when replaying history is a real requirement — not by default.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Service Discovery?

“Once services scale to many, constantly-changing instances, hardcoding “call this IP address” stops working — ____ is how one service finds a current, healthy instance of another without that address ever being hardcoded.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.explanation: Once services scale to many, constantly-changing instances, hardcoding “call this IP address” stops working — service discovery is how one service finds a current, healthy instance of another without that address ever being hardcoded.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Service Discovery?

“Each service instance registers itself with a ____ on startup, and removes itself (or is removed via health check) on shutdown.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.explanation: Each service instance registers itself with a service registry on startup, and removes itself (or is removed via health check) on shutdown.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Service Discovery?

“The orders ____ needs to call the inventory ____, which runs as a fleet of instances that scales up and down with load.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.explanation: The orders service needs to call the inventory service, which runs as a fleet of instances that scales up and down with load.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Service Discovery?

“Forgetting that the registry itself needs to be highly available — it becomes a ____ for practically every service-to-service call if it goes down.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.explanation: Forgetting that the registry itself needs to be highly available — it becomes a single point of failure for practically every service-to-service call if it goes down.

high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Service Discovery?

“When one service needs to call another, it asks the registry for a current list of healthy instances rather than using a fixed address — often paired with client-side ____ to pick one.”
high-level-design/distributed-systems--s.explanation: When one service needs to call another, it asks the registry for a current list of healthy instances rather than using a fixed address — often paired with client-side load balancing to pick one.

high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Fault Tolerance?

“In a system built from enough machines, something is statistically always failing somewhere — fault tolerance is the design habit of assuming that from the start, rather than treating every ____ as a surprise.”
high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.explanation: In a system built from enough machines, something is statistically always failing somewhere — fault tolerance is the design habit of assuming that from the start, rather than treating every failure as a surprise.

high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Fault Tolerance?

“It’s an umbrella that the rest of this section’s tools (____, circuit breakers, retries, disaster recovery) each implement a piece of: no single component’s failure should be able to take down the whole design, and every component that can fail should have a defined, deliberate behavior for when it does.”
high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.explanation: It’s an umbrella that the rest of this section’s tools (redundancy, circuit breakers, retries, disaster recovery) each implement a piece of: no single component’s failure should be able to take down the whole design, and every component that can fail should have a defined, deliberate behavior for when it does.

high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Fault Tolerance?

“Without fault tolerance: the ____ page itself fails to load, because it was written to require recommendations to succeed.”
high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.explanation: Without fault tolerance: the product page itself fails to load, because it was written to require recommendations to succeed.

high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Fault Tolerance?

“Making every ____ “required” by default, without asking whether it truly needs to block the primary function, turns every minor outage into a major one.”
high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.explanation: Making every dependency “required” by default, without asking whether it truly needs to block the primary function, turns every minor outage into a major one.

high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Fault Tolerance?

“____ tolerance is the discipline of deciding, for every dependency, what happens when it fails — before it actually does, in production, without a plan.”
high-level-design/reliability--fault-tol.explanation: Fault tolerance is the discipline of deciding, for every dependency, what happens when it fails — before it actually does, in production, without a plan.

high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Redundancy and Failover?

“____ means never having exactly one of anything critical; failover is the mechanism that actually switches traffic to the backup the moment the primary stops responding.”
high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.explanation: Redundancy means never having exactly one of anything critical; failover is the mechanism that actually switches traffic to the backup the moment the primary stops responding.

high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Redundancy and Failover?

“The two are always designed together: redundant instances (multiple API servers, replica databases, a secondary region), plus a mechanism — a load balancer’s health checks, a ____ protocol, DNS failover — that detects the failure and redirects traffic automatically, ideally within seconds and without a human in the loop.”
high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.explanation: The two are always designed together: redundant instances (multiple API servers, replica databases, a secondary region), plus a mechanism — a load balancer’s health checks, a leader election protocol, DNS failover — that detects the failure and redirects traffic automatically, ideally within seconds and without a human in the loop.

high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Redundancy and Failover?

“____ is a single point of failure — its loss takes down every write in the system.”
high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.explanation: A single database instance is a single point of failure — its loss takes down every write in the system.

high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Redundancy and Failover?

“Placing the redundant instance in the same failure domain as the primary (same rack, same ____ zone) also defeats much of the purpose — a single event can then take both down together.”
high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.explanation: Placing the redundant instance in the same failure domain as the primary (same rack, same availability zone) also defeats much of the purpose — a single event can then take both down together.

high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Redundancy and Failover?

“Redundancy and ____ are one design decision, not two — a backup is only as good as the tested, automatic mechanism that actually switches to it.”
high-level-design/reliability--redundanc.explanation: Redundancy and failover are one design decision, not two — a backup is only as good as the tested, automatic mechanism that actually switches to it.

high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Circuit Breakers?

“When a downstream service is struggling, continuing to hammer it with requests just makes things worse — a ____ stops calling a failing dependency for a while, giving it room to recover.”
high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.explanation: When a downstream service is struggling, continuing to hammer it with requests just makes things worse — a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency for a while, giving it room to recover.

high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Circuit Breakers?

“A circuit breaker wraps a call to a ____ and tracks its recent failure rate.”
high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.explanation: A circuit breaker wraps a call to a dependency and tracks its recent failure rate.

high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Circuit Breakers?

“The payments ____ starts timing out under load, and the checkout ____ keeps calling it anyway.”
high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.explanation: The payments service starts timing out under load, and the checkout service keeps calling it anyway.

high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Circuit Breakers?

“Skipping circuit breakers on calls to unreliable ____ lets one struggling service cascade failures into every service that calls it.”
high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.explanation: Skipping circuit breakers on calls to unreliable dependencies lets one struggling service cascade failures into every service that calls it.

high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Circuit Breakers?

“A circuit breaker stops a struggling dependency from taking the ____ of the system down with it — failing fast instead of failing slowly and expensively.”
high-level-design/reliability--circuit-b.explanation: A circuit breaker stops a struggling dependency from taking the rest of the system down with it — failing fast instead of failing slowly and expensively.

high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Retries and Backoff?

“Not every ____ is permanent — a lot of them are brief blips that succeed on a second attempt.”
high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.explanation: Not every failure is permanent — a lot of them are brief blips that succeed on a second attempt.

high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Retries and Backoff?

“____ waits progressively longer between attempts (1s, 2s, 4s...), and jitter randomizes that wait slightly so many clients retrying at once don’t all hit the dependency in synchronized waves.”
high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.explanation: Exponential backoff waits progressively longer between attempts (1s, 2s, 4s...), and jitter randomizes that wait slightly so many clients retrying at once don’t all hit the dependency in synchronized waves.

high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Retries and Backoff?

“A call to the inventory service fails due to a brief ____ blip.”
high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.explanation: A call to the inventory service fails due to a brief network blip.

high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Retries and Backoff?

“Retrying non-____ operations (like “charge this card”) without safeguards can also cause a customer to be charged twice.”
high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.explanation: Retrying non-idempotent operations (like “charge this card”) without safeguards can also cause a customer to be charged twice.

high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Retries and Backoff?

“Retries help with transient ____ only when they back off, add jitter, and eventually give up — an uncapped, immediate retry loop is a self-inflicted outage waiting to happen.”
high-level-design/reliability--retries-a.explanation: Retries help with transient failures only when they back off, add jitter, and eventually give up — an uncapped, immediate retry loop is a self-inflicted outage waiting to happen.

high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Disaster Recovery?

“Disaster recovery plans for the failure ____ alone can’t absorb — an entire region going down — and forces two explicit numbers onto the design: how much data you can afford to lose, and how long you can afford to be down.”
high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.explanation: Disaster recovery plans for the failure redundancy alone can’t absorb — an entire region going down — and forces two explicit numbers onto the design: how much data you can afford to lose, and how long you can afford to be down.

high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Disaster Recovery?

“____ is how much data loss is acceptable, measured in time — an RPO of 5 minutes means backups or replication must be frequent enough that at most 5 minutes of writes are ever at risk.”
high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.explanation: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is how much data loss is acceptable, measured in time — an RPO of 5 minutes means backups or replication must be frequent enough that at most 5 minutes of writes are ever at risk.

high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Disaster Recovery?

“The business states its tolerance: ____, RTO of 1 hour for the order database.”
high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.explanation: The business states its tolerance: RPO of 15 minutes, RTO of 1 hour for the order database.

high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Disaster Recovery?

“Agreeing to an RPO or RTO without checking whether the current ____ can actually meet it is the other common mistake — the numbers have to drive the design, not be promised independently of it.”
high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.explanation: Agreeing to an RPO or RTO without checking whether the current architecture can actually meet it is the other common mistake — the numbers have to drive the design, not be promised independently of it.

high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Disaster Recovery?

“____ and RTO turn “what if the whole region goes down” from a vague fear into two explicit numbers that the architecture is deliberately built to satisfy.”
high-level-design/reliability--disaster-.explanation: RPO and RTO turn “what if the whole region goes down” from a vague fear into two explicit numbers that the architecture is deliberately built to satisfy.

high-level-design/operations--authentica.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication and Authorization?

“____ verifies identity — a password, a token, a session — and typically happens once per session at the edge of the system (an API gateway or an auth service).”
high-level-design/operations--authentica.explanation: Authentication verifies identity — a password, a token, a session — and typically happens once per session at the edge of the system (an API gateway or an auth service).

high-level-design/operations--authentica.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication and Authorization?

“____ checks whether that already-verified identity is permitted to perform a specific action, and it can happen anywhere in the system, not just at the edge — a service deep in the call chain may still need to check permissions before acting.”
high-level-design/operations--authentica.explanation: Authorization checks whether that already-verified identity is permitted to perform a specific action, and it can happen anywhere in the system, not just at the edge — a service deep in the call chain may still need to check permissions before acting.

high-level-design/operations--authentica.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication and Authorization?

“The auth ____ verifies their credentials and issues a signed token identifying them — authentication, done once.”
high-level-design/operations--authentica.explanation: The auth service verifies their credentials and issues a signed token identifying them — authentication, done once.

high-level-design/operations--authentica.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication and Authorization?

“Checking authorization only at the API gateway, and trusting every internal service call afterward, leaves internal ____ with no defense if a request reaches them by an unexpected path.”
high-level-design/operations--authentica.explanation: Checking authorization only at the API gateway, and trusting every internal service call afterward, leaves internal services with no defense if a request reaches them by an unexpected path.

high-level-design/operations--authentica.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Authentication and Authorization?

“Treat authentication and authorization as two separate checks in the design — one established once per ____, the other checked at every point an action is actually attempted.”
high-level-design/operations--authentica.explanation: Treat authentication and authorization as two separate checks in the design — one established once per session, the other checked at every point an action is actually attempted.

high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“A rate limiter caps how many ____ a single client can make in a given window — protecting the system from a single misbehaving or overly aggressive caller, whether malicious or accidental.”
high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.explanation: A rate limiter caps how many requests a single client can make in a given window — protecting the system from a single misbehaving or overly aggressive caller, whether malicious or accidental.

high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“The token bucket algorithm is a common ____: each client has a bucket of tokens that refills at a steady rate, and each request consumes one; an empty bucket means the request is rejected until it refills.”
high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.explanation: The token bucket algorithm is a common implementation: each client has a bucket of tokens that refills at a steady rate, and each request consumes one; an empty bucket means the request is rejected until it refills.

high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Each API key gets a bucket of 100 ____, refilling at 10 ____ per second.”
high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.explanation: Each API key gets a bucket of 100 tokens, refilling at 10 tokens per second.

high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Applying one global rate limit across all ____, instead of a per-client limit, lets a single bad actor exhaust the entire budget for everyone else.”
high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.explanation: Applying one global rate limit across all clients, instead of a per-client limit, lets a single bad actor exhaust the entire budget for everyone else.

high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Rate Limiting?

“Rate limiting protects a system from any one ____ — well-meaning or not — consuming more than its fair share, without needing a human watching in real time.”
high-level-design/operations--rate-limit.explanation: Rate limiting protects a system from any one client — well-meaning or not — consuming more than its fair share, without needing a human watching in real time.

high-level-design/operations--observabil.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Observability?

“Observability is whether the system can actually answer “why is this happening” when something goes wrong in production — a ____ property, not something bolted on after an incident.”
high-level-design/operations--observabil.explanation: Observability is whether the system can actually answer “why is this happening” when something goes wrong in production — a design property, not something bolted on after an incident.

high-level-design/operations--observabil.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Observability?

“Observability rests on three pillars: ____ (numeric signals like request rate and error rate, cheap to collect continuously), logs (detailed records of specific events, useful for deep-diving one request), and traces (following one request across every service it touches, showing where time was spent).”
high-level-design/operations--observabil.explanation: Observability rests on three pillars: metrics (numeric signals like request rate and error rate, cheap to collect continuously), logs (detailed records of specific events, useful for deep-diving one request), and traces (following one request across every service it touches, showing where time was spent).

high-level-design/operations--observabil.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Observability?

“____ show nearly all their time is spent in a call to the payments service.”
high-level-design/operations--observabil.explanation: Traces for failing requests show nearly all their time is spent in a call to the payments service.

high-level-design/operations--observabil.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Observability?

“Relying on logs alone, without metrics or tracing, means every incident starts with grepping through text instead of jumping straight to the relevant ____.”
high-level-design/operations--observabil.explanation: Relying on logs alone, without metrics or tracing, means every incident starts with grepping through text instead of jumping straight to the relevant service.

high-level-design/operations--observabil.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Observability?

“Observability should appear on the component ____ itself, not just in an incident postmortem — every service should be built from the start to export what it takes to answer “why is this happening.””
high-level-design/operations--observabil.explanation: Observability should appear on the component diagram itself, not just in an incident postmortem — every service should be built from the start to export what it takes to answer “why is this happening.”

high-level-design/operations--logging-an.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Logging and Monitoring?

“Logging records what happened; ____ watches metrics continuously and tells someone when something needs attention — complementary, and both need a place in the design from the start.”
high-level-design/operations--logging-an.explanation: Logging records what happened; monitoring watches metrics continuously and tells someone when something needs attention — complementary, and both need a place in the design from the start.

high-level-design/operations--logging-an.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Logging and Monitoring?

“____ watches metrics continuously and pages a human when a threshold is crossed — ideally a threshold tied to actual user impact (error rate, latency) rather than an internal detail (CPU usage) that may or may not matter to anyone.”
high-level-design/operations--logging-an.explanation: Monitoring and alerting watches metrics continuously and pages a human when a threshold is crossed — ideally a threshold tied to actual user impact (error rate, latency) rather than an internal detail (CPU usage) that may or may not matter to anyone.

high-level-design/operations--logging-an.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Logging and Monitoring?

“____ with consistent fields: timestamp, request ID, service name, status.”
high-level-design/operations--logging-an.explanation: Every service emits structured logs with consistent fields: timestamp, request ID, service name, status.

high-level-design/operations--logging-an.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Logging and Monitoring?

“Free-form, unstructured log ____ are nearly impossible to search or aggregate at scale across many instances.”
high-level-design/operations--logging-an.explanation: Free-form, unstructured log messages are nearly impossible to search or aggregate at scale across many instances.

high-level-design/operations--logging-an.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Logging and Monitoring?

“Structured, aggregated ____ and symptom-based monitoring together turn “something feels wrong” into a specific alert and a searchable trail to the cause.”
high-level-design/operations--logging-an.explanation: Structured, aggregated logging and symptom-based monitoring together turn “something feels wrong” into a specific alert and a searchable trail to the cause.

high-level-design/operations--deployment.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Deployment Strategy?

“Shipping a new version of a service is itself a moment of risk — ____ strategy is how a design rolls out change without exposing every user to a bad release at once.”
high-level-design/operations--deployment.explanation: Shipping a new version of a service is itself a moment of risk — deployment strategy is how a design rolls out change without exposing every user to a bad release at once.

high-level-design/operations--deployment.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Deployment Strategy?

“A new version of the checkout ____ is ready to deploy.”
high-level-design/operations--deployment.explanation: A new version of the checkout service is ready to deploy.

high-level-design/operations--deployment.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Deployment Strategy?

“Route 5% of real ____ to the new version (a canary), leaving 95% on the current, known-good version.”
high-level-design/operations--deployment.explanation: Route 5% of real traffic to the new version (a canary), leaving 95% on the current, known-good version.

high-level-design/operations--deployment.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Deployment Strategy?

“Watching a ____ without a clear, pre-agreed threshold for what counts as “bad enough to roll back” also delays the decision when something does go wrong.”
high-level-design/operations--deployment.explanation: Watching a canary without a clear, pre-agreed threshold for what counts as “bad enough to roll back” also delays the decision when something does go wrong.

high-level-design/operations--deployment.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Deployment Strategy?

“A good deployment ____ limits how many users a bad release can reach before it’s caught — the goal is always an early, cheap warning instead of a late, expensive one.”
high-level-design/operations--deployment.explanation: A good deployment strategy limits how many users a bad release can reach before it’s caught — the goal is always an early, cheap warning instead of a late, expensive one.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a URL Shortener?

““Given a long URL, return a short one that redirects back to it.” It’s often the very first system design question a candidate hears, precisely because it’s small enough to finish in one session — which means the interviewer isn’t grading scope, they’re grading whether you notice this is a wildly ____ service and design the write path accordingly.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: “Given a long URL, return a short one that redirects back to it.” It’s often the very first system design question a candidate hears, precisely because it’s small enough to finish in one session — which means the interviewer isn’t grading scope, they’re grading whether you notice this is a wildly read-heavy service and design the write path accordingly.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a URL Shortener?

“____ are short: turn a long URL into a short code, redirect visitors from the short code back to the original, and optionally support a custom alias or an expiry date.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Functional requirements are short: turn a long URL into a short code, redirect visitors from the short code back to the original, and optionally support a custom alias or an expiry date.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a URL Shortener?

“The app ____ handling the request already holds a locally-claimed block of IDs, so it takes the next free one without talking to any other ____.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: The app server handling the request already holds a locally-claimed block of IDs, so it takes the next free one without talking to any other server.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a URL Shortener?

“Skipping the cache because “it’s just a lookup” ignores that reads can outnumber writes a thousand to one, so the datastore becomes the ____ without one.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Skipping the cache because “it’s just a lookup” ignores that reads can outnumber writes a thousand to one, so the datastore becomes the bottleneck without one.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a URL Shortener?

“A small-sounding prompt is really a test of read/write judgment: get ID generation off the write path’s critical section and put a cache in front of the read path, and the rest of the ____ falls out on its own.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: A small-sounding prompt is really a test of read/write judgment: get ID generation off the write path’s critical section and put a cache in front of the read path, and the rest of the design falls out on its own.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Social Feed?

““Show me posts from the people I follow, newest first.” The ____ side of this is easy — a table of posts and a table of follows.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: “Show me posts from the people I follow, newest first.” The storage side of this is easy — a table of posts and a table of follows.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Social Feed?

“The tradeoff that defines the system is ____ versus fan-out-on-read.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: The tradeoff that defines the system is fan-out-on-write versus fan-out-on-read.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Social Feed?

“The post is saved, then a fan-out worker looks up its ____ list and pushes the post’s ID into each ____’s precomputed feed.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: The post is saved, then a fan-out worker looks up its follower list and pushes the post’s ID into each follower’s precomputed feed.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Social Feed?

“Treating the feed as a live query over the entire posts ____ on every load is the simplest thing to build, but doesn’t survive a follow graph of any real size.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Treating the feed as a live query over the entire posts table on every load is the simplest thing to build, but doesn’t survive a follow graph of any real size.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Social Feed?

“Match the fan-out ____ to the shape of the account, not the platform as a whole — that one hybrid decision is what keeps the feed both fast to read and survivable to write.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Match the fan-out strategy to the shape of the account, not the platform as a whole — that one hybrid decision is what keeps the feed both fast to read and survivable to write.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Chat System?

““Two users should be able to exchange ____ in real time.” What sets this apart from a typical CRUD service is that the server has to push data to one specific, already-connected client — not just answer whichever request happens to arrive.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: “Two users should be able to exchange messages in real time.” What sets this apart from a typical CRUD service is that the server has to push data to one specific, already-connected client — not just answer whichever request happens to arrive.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Chat System?

“A plain request/response cycle can’t push a message to a client that isn’t currently asking for one, so clients hold open a ____ (a WebSocket) to a chat server, and that server keeps track of which of its open connections belongs to which user.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: A plain request/response cycle can’t push a message to a client that isn’t currently asking for one, so clients hold open a persistent connection (a WebSocket) to a chat server, and that server keeps track of which of its open connections belongs to which user.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Chat System?

“Alice's client opens a persistent connection to whichever chat server the ____ assigns her to; that server records “Alice → this server” in the connection registry.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Alice's client opens a persistent connection to whichever chat server the load balancer assigns her to; that server records “Alice → this server” in the connection registry.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Chat System?

“Skipping the reconnection step is the third: without a backlog sync, a client that briefly drops its ____ silently misses everything sent in between.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Skipping the reconnection step is the third: without a backlog sync, a client that briefly drops its connection silently misses everything sent in between.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Chat System?

“Real-time delivery is a routing and state-tracking problem sitting on top of ordinary ____ — get the connection registry right and both the online and offline paths follow from it.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Real-time delivery is a routing and state-tracking problem sitting on top of ordinary storage — get the connection registry right and both the online and offline paths follow from it.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Video Platform?

““A creator uploads a video; viewers around the world watch it.” Almost the entire design problem lives between those two ____ — what happens to a video after it’s uploaded and before it’s actually watchable.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: “A creator uploads a video; viewers around the world watch it.” Almost the entire design problem lives between those two events — what happens to a video after it’s uploaded and before it’s actually watchable.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Video Platform?

“____: accept large uploads, make each video watchable at whatever resolution a viewer’s connection can handle, and serve viewing traffic globally without every request landing on one origin.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Requirements: accept large uploads, make each video watchable at whatever resolution a viewer’s connection can handle, and serve viewing traffic globally without every request landing on one origin.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Video Platform?

“It's written to ____, and an event is emitted — the upload request itself doesn't do any processing.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: It's written to object storage, and an event is emitted — the upload request itself doesn't do any processing.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Video Platform?

“Serving video bytes straight from application or origin ____ on every view defeats the purpose of a CDN, whose entire job is to serve popular content from near the viewer instead of refetching it from origin each time.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Serving video bytes straight from application or origin servers on every view defeats the purpose of a CDN, whose entire job is to serve popular content from near the viewer instead of refetching it from origin each time.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Video Platform?

“The whole design is a story of decoupling — bytes from metadata, upload from processing, and viewer traffic from the origin — with each split resolving a different ____.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: The whole design is a story of decoupling — bytes from metadata, upload from processing, and viewer traffic from the origin — with each split resolving a different bottleneck.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Ride-Sharing Service?

““Match a rider requesting a trip with a nearby available driver.” Unlike most systems in this course, the state that matters most here — a driver’s location — ____ every few seconds and only the latest value is ever useful, which pushes several design choices in a different direction than usual.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: “Match a rider requesting a trip with a nearby available driver.” Unlike most systems in this course, the state that matters most here — a driver’s location — changes every few seconds and only the latest value is ever useful, which pushes several design choices in a different direction than usual.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Ride-Sharing Service?

“____: drivers continuously report their location, riders request a trip, the system finds and confirms a nearby available driver, and both sides see live position updates once the trip starts.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Requirements: drivers continuously report their location, riders request a trip, the system finds and confirms a nearby available driver, and both sides see live position updates once the trip starts.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Ride-Sharing Service?

“Every few seconds, each driver's app reports its ____, overwriting that driver's previous position in a geospatial index keyed by grid cell — there's no history to keep, only a current value.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Every few seconds, each driver's app reports its coordinates, overwriting that driver's previous position in a geospatial index keyed by grid cell — there's no history to keep, only a current value.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Ride-Sharing Service?

“Skipping the lock step and offering, or worse confirming, the same driver to more than one rider at once is a ____ waiting to happen under real concurrency.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Skipping the lock step and offering, or worse confirming, the same driver to more than one rider at once is a race condition waiting to happen under real concurrency.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Ride-Sharing Service?

“When the data that matters is “the latest value, right now” rather than a durable record, the storage and indexing choices look different from the rest of this course — and the matching step still needs its own ____ guard on top.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: When the data that matters is “the latest value, right now” rather than a durable record, the storage and indexing choices look different from the rest of this course — and the matching step still needs its own concurrency guard on top.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Notification System?

““When something happens in the ____, tell the affected user — by push, email, or text.” The constraint that shapes this design is that whatever detects the event, say an order shipping, must never be slowed down or broken by a flaky third-party provider on the other end.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: “When something happens in the product, tell the affected user — by push, email, or text.” The constraint that shapes this design is that whatever detects the event, say an order shipping, must never be slowed down or broken by a flaky third-party provider on the other end.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Notification System?

“____: many different internal events can trigger a notification, a user may receive one over several channels, users have preferences (which channels, quiet hours), and an outage in one channel's provider shouldn't touch the others or the service that triggered the notification in the first place.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Requirements: many different internal events can trigger a notification, a user may receive one over several channels, users have preferences (which channels, quiet hours), and an outage in one channel's provider shouldn't touch the others or the service that triggered the notification in the first place.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Notification System?

“The orders ____ marks an order shipped and publishes an “order.shipped” event to a queue — its own request finishes right away, regardless of what happens next.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: The orders service marks an order shipped and publishes an “order.shipped” event to a queue — its own request finishes right away, regardless of what happens next.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Notification System?

“Treating every channel and every ____ as equally urgent, with user preferences and quiet hours bolted on as an afterthought, is the third.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: Treating every channel and every notification as equally urgent, with user preferences and quiet hours bolted on as an afterthought, is the third.

high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Design a Notification System?

“The queue in the middle is what lets the rest of the product move on immediately, while notification delivery — with all its ____ and third-party flakiness — happens entirely off to the side.”
high-level-design/hld-case-studies--desi.explanation: The queue in the middle is what lets the rest of the product move on immediately, while notification delivery — with all its retries and third-party flakiness — happens entirely off to the side.

low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Introduction?

“Low level design is the next step down: once you know a “PaymentService” box needs to exist, LLD is what decides what’s actually inside it — which ____, which responsibilities, which relationships.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.explanation: Low level design is the next step down: once you know a “PaymentService” box needs to exist, LLD is what decides what’s actually inside it — which classes, which responsibilities, which relationships.

low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Introduction?

“Where HLD reasons about services, databases, and network boundaries at the scale of an entire system, LLD reasons about objects: their fields, their methods, and how instances of different classes collaborate to fulfill one component’s ____.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.explanation: Where HLD reasons about services, databases, and network boundaries at the scale of an entire system, LLD reasons about objects: their fields, their methods, and how instances of different classes collaborate to fulfill one component’s responsibility.

low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Introduction?

“An HLD answer to “design a parking lot” might discuss a payments service, a ____ service, and a database that scales across multiple physical locations.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.explanation: An HLD answer to “design a parking lot” might discuss a payments service, a notifications service, and a database that scales across multiple physical locations.

low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Introduction?

“Jumping straight to code before sketching responsibilities and relationships is the other common ____; the classes that come out tend to be harder to explain and harder to extend.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.explanation: Jumping straight to code before sketching responsibilities and relationships is the other common failure; the classes that come out tend to be harder to explain and harder to extend.

low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Introduction?

“High level ____ decides which boxes exist in a system and how they talk to each other.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-introdu.explanation: High level design decides which boxes exist in a system and how they talk to each other.

low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Roadmap?

“This course moves from the raw material of object-oriented design up to fully worked ____ problems — each section is a tool, and the case studies at the end are where every tool gets used together on one problem at a time.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.explanation: This course moves from the raw material of object-oriented design up to fully worked interview problems — each section is a tool, and the case studies at the end are where every tool gets used together on one problem at a time.

low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Roadmap?

“Implementation Practices covers the practical concerns — error handling, concurrency, ____, testing — that separate a design that merely compiles from one that survives real changes.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.explanation: Implementation Practices covers the practical concerns — error handling, concurrency, dependency injection, testing — that separate a design that merely compiles from one that survives real changes.

low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Roadmap?

“LLD Foundations gives you the vocabulary — turning ____ into classes, naming how objects relate, and choosing composition over inheritance where it fits.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.explanation: LLD Foundations gives you the vocabulary — turning requirements into classes, naming how objects relate, and choosing composition over inheritance where it fits.

low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Roadmap?

“Skipping straight to design patterns without the SOLID ____ underneath leaves you applying a pattern without understanding which problem it actually solves.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.explanation: Skipping straight to design patterns without the SOLID foundations underneath leaves you applying a pattern without understanding which problem it actually solves.

low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Course Roadmap?

“SOLID Principles gives you the standards a good class ____ should meet.”
low-level-design/welcome--course-roadmap.explanation: SOLID Principles gives you the standards a good class design should meet.

low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from How to Approach LLD?

“The nouns in the ____ are your starting point — not every noun earns a class, but most classes start as a noun.”
low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.explanation: The nouns in the requirements are your starting point — not every noun earns a class, but most classes start as a noun.

low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from How to Approach LLD?

“Give each class one clear job before worrying about ____ or fields.”
low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.explanation: Give each class one clear job before worrying about methods or fields.

low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from How to Approach LLD?

“For “design a vending machine,” the first three steps might look like: scope is a single machine, one ____ at a time, no networked payment; candidate classes are VendingMachine, Product, and Coin; VendingMachine owns the ____ flow, Product owns its own price and stock count, Coin only represents a value.”
low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.explanation: For “design a vending machine,” the first three steps might look like: scope is a single machine, one transaction at a time, no networked payment; candidate classes are VendingMachine, Product, and Coin; VendingMachine owns the transaction flow, Product owns its own price and stock count, Coin only represents a value.

low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from How to Approach LLD?

“Designing the full class hierarchy before writing down what the system is actually required to do leads to elegant ____ that solve the wrong problem.”
low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.explanation: Designing the full class hierarchy before writing down what the system is actually required to do leads to elegant classes that solve the wrong problem.

low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from How to Approach LLD?

“Scope, classes, responsibilities, relationships, patterns, ____ — in that order, the same six steps carry you through almost any LLD prompt.”
low-level-design/welcome--how-to-approac.explanation: Scope, classes, responsibilities, relationships, patterns, sketch — in that order, the same six steps carry you through almost any LLD prompt.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is Low Level Design??

“Low level design turns a component’s responsibilities into a concrete object model — the ____ that exist, what each one knows and does, and how instances of those ____ collaborate.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.explanation: Low level design turns a component’s responsibilities into a concrete object model — the classes that exist, what each one knows and does, and how instances of those classes collaborate.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is Low Level Design??

“The usual artifacts are a class diagram (structure), sometimes a ____ (behavior for one scenario), and clear interfaces between the pieces.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.explanation: The usual artifacts are a class diagram (structure), sometimes a sequence diagram (behavior for one scenario), and clear interfaces between the pieces.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is Low Level Design??

“Take one requirement: “a member can check out a book.” Turning that into LLD means deciding there's a Book class (title, author), that “check out” is a method that probably lives on a Library or Loan class rather than on Book itself, and that the operation needs to check ____ before it succeeds.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.explanation: Take one requirement: “a member can check out a book.” Turning that into LLD means deciding there's a Book class (title, author), that “check out” is a method that probably lives on a Library or Loan class rather than on Book itself, and that the operation needs to check availability before it succeeds.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is Low Level Design??

“Treating LLD as UML-drawing for its own sake, disconnected from how the objects actually behave, produces ____ that look thorough but don't help anyone write or review the code.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.explanation: Treating LLD as UML-drawing for its own sake, disconnected from how the objects actually behave, produces diagrams that look thorough but don't help anyone write or review the code.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from What is Low Level Design??

“A good LLD is detailed enough that writing the actual code becomes close to transcription — the hard decisions (who's responsible for what, how ____ relate) are already made.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--what-i.explanation: A good LLD is detailed enough that writing the actual code becomes close to transcription — the hard decisions (who's responsible for what, how objects relate) are already made.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from From Requirements to Classes?

“____ arrive as sentences; a design needs classes.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.explanation: Requirements arrive as sentences; a design needs classes.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from From Requirements to Classes?

“The mechanical part stops there — not every noun deserves its own class, and related data and ____ should usually be grouped rather than split just because two different words were used for them.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.explanation: The mechanical part stops there — not every noun deserves its own class, and related data and behavior should usually be grouped rather than split just because two different words were used for them.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from From Requirements to Classes?

“Verbs: borrow, add — candidate methods: something like ____ and addBook().”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.explanation: Verbs: borrow, add — candidate methods: something like borrowBook() and addBook().

low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from From Requirements to Classes?

“Creating a class for every noun mechanically — including ones like “due date” that are really just a field — produces anemic ____ that hold data but no meaningful behavior of their own.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.explanation: Creating a class for every noun mechanically — including ones like “due date” that are really just a field — produces anemic classes that hold data but no meaningful behavior of their own.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from From Requirements to Classes?

“Nouns and verbs are a starting draft, not a final answer — the judgment is in deciding which nouns deserve a ____ and which relationships need one the sentence never spelled out.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--from-r.explanation: Nouns and verbs are a starting draft, not a final answer — the judgment is in deciding which nouns deserve a class and which relationships need one the sentence never spelled out.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Objects and Relationships?

“Once you have candidate ____, the next question is how their instances relate to each other — and “has-a” hides at least three genuinely different relationships that behave differently when an object is destroyed.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.explanation: Once you have candidate classes, the next question is how their instances relate to each other — and “has-a” hides at least three genuinely different relationships that behave differently when an object is destroyed.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Objects and Relationships?

“And a method signature like ____ is a dependency — the class needs a Logger for this one call, not as a lasting part of its own structure.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.explanation: And a method signature like process(Logger logger) is a dependency — the class needs a Logger for this one call, not as a lasting part of its own structure.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Objects and Relationships?

“A Car being scrapped does take its specific Engine instance with it — nobody reuses one car’s physical engine object as another car’s (____).”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.explanation: A Car being scrapped does take its specific Engine instance with it — nobody reuses one car’s physical engine object as another car’s (composition).

low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Objects and Relationships?

“Overusing ____ where one of these has-a relationships would model reality more accurately is the other common misstep, and it's exactly what the next article addresses directly.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.explanation: Overusing inheritance where one of these has-a relationships would model reality more accurately is the other common misstep, and it's exactly what the next article addresses directly.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Objects and Relationships?

“A Driver ____ simply calling car.start() is association — the Driver doesn’t own the Car’s lifetime at all.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--object.explanation: A Driver object simply calling car.start() is association — the Driver doesn’t own the Car’s lifetime at all.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encapsulation and Abstraction?

“____ and abstraction get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but they solve two different problems: one protects an object's state, the other hides a system's complexity behind a simpler contract.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.explanation: Encapsulation and abstraction get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but they solve two different problems: one protects an object's state, the other hides a system's complexity behind a simpler contract.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encapsulation and Abstraction?

“Abstraction exposes only the essential behavior through an interface, hiding ____ details entirely — a caller depends on what a class does, never how it does it.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.explanation: Abstraction exposes only the essential behavior through an interface, hiding implementation details entirely — a caller depends on what a class does, never how it does it.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encapsulation and Abstraction?

“A concrete ____ implementing that interface is where encapsulation applies: its API keys and HTTP client are private fields, never exposed as public getters, so swapping the HTTP library later doesn’t touch a single caller.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.explanation: A concrete StripePaymentProcessor implementing that interface is where encapsulation applies: its API keys and HTTP client are private fields, never exposed as public getters, so swapping the HTTP library later doesn’t touch a single caller.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encapsulation and Abstraction?

“Conflating an “abstract class” the language feature with “____” the design principle is a common vocabulary slip; you can write a perfectly good ____ with no abstract class in sight, and a badly encapsulated one that happens to use one.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.explanation: Conflating an “abstract class” the language feature with “abstraction” the design principle is a common vocabulary slip; you can write a perfectly good abstraction with no abstract class in sight, and a badly encapsulated one that happens to use one.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Encapsulation and Abstraction?

“Encapsulation protects an object's state from the outside; abstraction hides a system's complexity behind a simpler ____.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--encaps.explanation: Encapsulation protects an object's state from the outside; abstraction hides a system's complexity behind a simpler contract.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Composition vs Inheritance?

“Inheritance models “is-a” and gives you ____ for free, but it can quietly lock a class into behavior it can’t escape as requirements change — which is exactly why “favor composition over inheritance” is one of the most repeated pieces of design advice.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.explanation: Inheritance models “is-a” and gives you polymorphism for free, but it can quietly lock a class into behavior it can’t escape as requirements change — which is exactly why “favor composition over inheritance” is one of the most repeated pieces of design advice.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Composition vs Inheritance?

“Inheritance couples a subclass tightly to its superclass’s ____, and deep hierarchies become fragile as new cases appear that don’t cleanly fit the existing tree.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.explanation: Inheritance couples a subclass tightly to its superclass’s implementation, and deep hierarchies become fragile as new cases appear that don’t cleanly fit the existing tree.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Composition vs Inheritance?

“The fix is composition: give Duck a FlyBehavior field instead of a fixed fly() method — a real duck is composed with a ____ behavior, a rubber duck with a CannotFly behavior, and new duck types just get assigned whichever behavior actually fits, with no restructuring required.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.explanation: The fix is composition: give Duck a FlyBehavior field instead of a fixed fly() method — a real duck is composed with a FlyWithWings behavior, a rubber duck with a CannotFly behavior, and new duck types just get assigned whichever behavior actually fits, with no restructuring required.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Composition vs Inheritance?

“Using ____ purely for code reuse, with no genuine is-a relationship behind it, is the single most common source of fragile hierarchies.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.explanation: Using inheritance purely for code reuse, with no genuine is-a relationship behind it, is the single most common source of fragile hierarchies.

low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Composition vs Inheritance?

“Reach for inheritance only for a genuine, stable is-a relationship; reach for ____ when behavior needs to vary or swap at runtime — which, in practice, is most of the time.”
low-level-design/lld-foundations--compos.explanation: Reach for inheritance only for a genuine, stable is-a relationship; reach for composition when behavior needs to vary or swap at runtime — which, in practice, is most of the time.

low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Responsibility Principle?

“A class should have exactly one reason to change — one ____, answering to one actor or concern.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.explanation: A class should have exactly one reason to change — one responsibility, answering to one actor or concern.

low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Responsibility Principle?

“The test is whether the class would need to change for more than one unrelated reason: if pricing logic, print formatting, and ____ format each independently might change, and all three live in the same class, that class has three reasons to change, not one.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.explanation: The test is whether the class would need to change for more than one unrelated reason: if pricing logic, print formatting, and storage format each independently might change, and all three live in the same class, that class has three reasons to change, not one.

low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Responsibility Principle?

“Splitting it into Invoice (data and calculation), InvoicePrinter, and ____ means each class now changes for exactly one of those reasons, and changing the print layout can never accidentally break the tax calculation.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.explanation: Splitting it into Invoice (data and calculation), InvoicePrinter, and InvoiceRepository means each class now changes for exactly one of those reasons, and changing the print layout can never accidentally break the tax calculation.

low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Responsibility Principle?

“Confusing “one responsibility” with “one method” leads to needless splitting of ____ that already had a single, cohesive concern spread across several related methods.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.explanation: Confusing “one responsibility” with “one method” leads to needless splitting of classes that already had a single, cohesive concern spread across several related methods.

low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Single Responsibility Principle?

“Ask whether a class would need to change for more than one unrelated reason — that's the real test for single responsibility, not how many ____ it has.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--singl.explanation: Ask whether a class would need to change for more than one unrelated reason — that's the real test for single responsibility, not how many methods it has.

low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Open Closed Principle?

“A class should be open for extension but closed for modification — you should be able to add new ____ without editing and re-testing code that already works.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.explanation: A class should be open for extension but closed for modification — you should be able to add new behavior without editing and re-testing code that already works.

low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Open Closed Principle?

“The usual fix is polymorphism: define an interface for the varying behavior, put each case behind its own ____, and have the calling code depend only on the interface — adding a case means adding a new class, never touching the ones that already shipped.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.explanation: The usual fix is polymorphism: define an interface for the varying behavior, put each case behind its own implementation, and have the calling code depend only on the interface — adding a case means adding a new class, never touching the ones that already shipped.

low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Open Closed Principle?

“A ____ with an if/else chain checking customer.type against “regular”, “premium”, and “vip” means adding a new tier requires editing that method and re-testing every existing branch alongside it.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.explanation: A DiscountCalculator with an if/else chain checking customer.type against “regular”, “premium”, and “vip” means adding a new tier requires editing that method and re-testing every existing branch alongside it.

low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Open Closed Principle?

“Applying OCP preemptively everywhere — abstracting behavior that has never actually needed a second variant — adds indirection for ____ that may never come. “Closed for modification” is a response to a demonstrated pattern of ____, not a mandate to abstract every class up front.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.explanation: Applying OCP preemptively everywhere — abstracting behavior that has never actually needed a second variant — adds indirection for change that may never come. “Closed for modification” is a response to a demonstrated pattern of change, not a mandate to abstract every class up front.

low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Open Closed Principle?

“When a branch keeps growing with every new case, that's the signal to close it off behind an ____ — not a reason to abstract everything else in anticipation.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--open-.explanation: When a branch keeps growing with every new case, that's the signal to close it off behind an interface — not a reason to abstract everything else in anticipation.

low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Liskov Substitution Principle?

“A ____ must be usable anywhere its superclass is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions — a subtype has to honor the parent's contract, not just match its method signatures.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.explanation: A subclass must be usable anywhere its superclass is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions — a subtype has to honor the parent's contract, not just match its method signatures.

low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Liskov Substitution Principle?

“LSP is about ____: if code written against the superclass would break when handed a specific subclass instead, that subclass isn’t a valid substitute — regardless of whether it compiles cleanly and looks like a reasonable “is-a” in English.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.explanation: LSP is about behavior: if code written against the superclass would break when handed a specific subclass instead, that subclass isn’t a valid substitute — regardless of whether it compiles cleanly and looks like a reasonable “is-a” in English.

low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Liskov Substitution Principle?

“Rectangle has independent setWidth() and ____ methods, and any caller of Rectangle reasonably assumes setting one leaves the other unchanged.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.explanation: Rectangle has independent setWidth() and setHeight() methods, and any caller of Rectangle reasonably assumes setting one leaves the other unchanged.

low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Liskov Substitution Principle?

“Checking only that method signatures match, without checking that behavioral contracts and ____ still hold, misses exactly the class of bug LSP exists to catch.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.explanation: Checking only that method signatures match, without checking that behavioral contracts and invariants still hold, misses exactly the class of bug LSP exists to catch.

low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Liskov Substitution Principle?

“A valid subtype honors its parent's behavioral ____, not just its method signatures — an "is-a" relationship in English doesn't guarantee that on its own.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--lisko.explanation: A valid subtype honors its parent's behavioral contract, not just its method signatures — an "is-a" relationship in English doesn't guarantee that on its own.

low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Interface Segregation Principle?

“No client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use — several small, focused ____ beat one broad interface that tries to serve every implementer at once.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.explanation: No client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use — several small, focused interfaces beat one broad interface that tries to serve every implementer at once.

low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Interface Segregation Principle?

“A “fat” ____ bundles methods that make sense for some implementers but not others, forcing the ones that don’t need a method to implement it anyway — usually as a no-op or a thrown exception, both of which are warning signs that the ____ is doing too much.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.explanation: A “fat” interface bundles methods that make sense for some implementers but not others, forcing the ones that don’t need a method to implement it anyway — usually as a no-op or a thrown exception, both of which are warning signs that the interface is doing too much.

low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Interface Segregation Principle?

“Splitting into Workable (just work() ) and Eatable (just eat() ) lets Robot implement only Workable, while a ____ implements both.”
low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.explanation: Splitting into Workable (just work() ) and Eatable (just eat() ) lets Robot implement only Workable, while a HumanWorker implements both.

low-level-design/solid-principles--inter.prompt:
Which term completes this statement from Interface Segregation Principle?

“Overcorrecting into dozens of one-method interfaces, when a small cohesive group of ____ always travels together anyway, trades one problem for a different kind of clutter.”
